CLI installable, that's fine." So SQLite was considered and is **not** wanted, and CordyOSS §7.2's
managed-Postgres recommendation already matches the intent. Never propose a second storage backend.

**Why that is cheaper than §7.2 implies** (measured 2026-08-13, not in the repo): app records are
already behind `IEntityStore` with a Postgres and an in-memory implementation. The genuinely
Postgres-shaped pieces — `pg_advisory` locks, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` as the turn-stream broker,
`tenant_{id}` schema-per-tenant — exist to coordinate **separate api/worker/ops hosts**. A
single-process local runtime drops them rather than porting them. The real remaining cost is the
control plane: EF Core + Npgsql, ~30 migrations, 26 `jsonb` column declarations.

**THE FILE FORMAT IS DECLARATIVE YAML, NOT OPERATIONS** (corrected and SHIPPED 2026-08-13). An
operation is a command log; source is a declaration. Ops exist because whole-DOCUMENT rewriting caused
destructive omissions on a 208KB AppDefinition — that lesson does not transfer to a 200-line
per-aggregate file, and a dropped field is caught by `git diff` locally and the diff screen in the
product. The ops layer is ~2,700 lines that may now largely die.

**`CordSource` is the format and it is TOTAL.** The forcing measurement: `CordDocument.Write` had
unwritable pointers for ALL 15 reference apps — an op cannot express a raw fragment and the whole
visual layer is one — so nothing could be written to files, and `CoCreationStore`'s
`if (!materialized.Complete) return []` means **every imported hosted app has zero `.cord` file rows
right now**. CordSource splits the LOWERED document, so it is total by construction and exactly
invertible (`Join(Split(d)) == d` by definition hash, asserted for all 15). A declaration may carry raw
where an operation may not — that rule is about what a MODEL emits, and a file writer is not in any
tool schema. **Three layers: CordSource = format (pure, no YAML — rule 0), `Cli/Workspace/Yaml.cs` =
syntax, `AppFolder` = filesystem.**

**The spec is `examples/semantic/budgetPlanner/`, and `verify.py` is what makes it one.** `generate.mjs --check` only
asks "are these the files the generator would write" — it blesses a lossy generator. `verify.py`
rebuilds the AppDefinition FROM the YAML and asserts values + array order against the authority. Run it
after any format change. **Entity files are DOMAIN ONLY**; `detail`/`peek`/`form` live in
`views/entities/<key>/` with tabs one file each (Tim couldn't find the scenario detail because it was
hidden in the entity — 32% of an entity file was layout).

**YAML's real risk is SILENT, not loud** (I claimed the opposite once; wrong). The specimen shipped
`on: record.created` parsing as boolean `true` in all 6 automations, and `unit:  yr` losing its leading
space. Both parse cleanly and mean something else. A generated writer quotes by construction — which is
the argument for CordSource owning the bytes rather than hand-editing being the primary path.

**THE RECURRING FAILURE IS "RIGHT DECISION, UNREACHABLE REASON."** Every live agent report (three in
one day, 2026-08-13) was this: the cron rule was in the op schema, the operation schemas were
`internal`, the synthesized command key was in the manifest not the definition, `createForEach` was a
documented deliberate exclusion. Only `contains` and `pie` were genuine gaps. **Check whether an
absence is deliberate BEFORE widening anything** — I twice nearly reversed an evidence-backed decision
(`command` on a transition: "52 of 52 corpus commands" say it is derived; effect types: a documented
DELIBERATE SUBSET). Now structural: `CordWordMap.Withheld` carries each withheld value + reason, `cord
vocabulary` prints them, and `Every_value_the_platform_accepts_is_offered_or_withheld_on_purpose`
fails the build if a platform value is neither offered nor explained.

**AN AGENT WILL GO INTO THE BINARY IF YOU DON'T GIVE IT A VOCABULARY CHANNEL** (observed live
2026-08-13). Claude Code wanted a calendar view's setting names, had no way to ask, and scraped
strings out of `cord.exe` — heading for the whole 143 KB schema next. **It was right to**: Cord models
the domain and NOT screens, so `views/` files are raw App Definition block trees with no semantic
vocabulary and no schema in the workspace. Fixed with `cord vocabulary` (index 1.6 KB, one block 5.2
KB, `$ref`s named not inlined) + a CLAUDE.md rule forbidding the binary route. **It is a workaround
for the 53% coverage, not a feature** — modelling screens removes the need. Treat "the agent did
something weird" as a missing-channel diagnosis first.

**Two design decisions that will look arbitrary later:**

- **"Accept" is Git.** Rule 10 says only a user action writes accepted source. In a checkout the
  working tree IS the candidate — `cord apply` writes there, a person reads `git diff`, staging is
  the acceptance. Do NOT add a `.cord.candidate/` shadow tree; it is a weaker VCS on top of a
  stronger one.
- **There is no parser.** File format v1 IS the operation vocabulary, so `CordFiles.Join` +
  `CordTransaction.Prepare` are the reader. The §3.5 YAML-vs-JSONC decision is therefore not
  blocking anything.

**Next = phase 2, the packaged cross-platform Postgres spike**, which the plan itself calls the
highest-risk slice. Watch for: `initdb` refusing to run as root, macOS notarization covering the
bundled Postgres binaries (curl-installed files dodge Gatekeeper quarantine; a `.pkg` would not),
and the Linux glibc + **libicu** baseline, which is the one that silently breaks collations.
Candidate binary source to evaluate first: zonky.io `embedded-postgres-binaries`.

Related: [[cord-co-creation-plan]] (the hosted host of the same `CordWorkspace` engine),
[[cord-semantic-authoring]], [[use-docker-for-services]].

content.text:
I've completed the restructuring phase of the plan (slices S0–S3). The open-source core is no longer a claim about the dependency graph — it physically lives in your three GitHub repositories, and the extraction test is a command that runs against a clone with nothing of the platform above it.

## What shipped

**The three repos are mounted as submodules** at `oss/cordango`, `oss/web-controls`, `oss/examples`, each with Apache-2.0, a README, and a `.gitattributes` forcing LF — without that last one, Git for Windows' system-wide `core.autocrlf=true` would hand a fresh clone CRLF files and quietly break the byte-determinism promise the generator is built on.

**`Cordango.Compiler`** merges the old Definition and Cord projects and takes with them the five genuinely pure files from Runtime (`AppCompiler`, `CandidateValidator`, `OpenApiFromManifest`, `SeedPlan`, `SeedRows`), plus condition and template evaluation as `Cordango.Semantics`. The schema, the composer inputs, the core-app registry and the whole 15-app conformance corpus went with it.

**`Cordango.Authorization` is the one deliberate addition to your tree.** `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` came out of Runtime into a project with zero package references. Your review asked for a shared authorization core rather than two implementations, and the separate project is what lets a generated app answer "may this role read this field" without inheriting a 213 KB JSON Schema and a validator to do it.

**The CLI lost its database driver.** It had referenced Runtime for `CandidateValidator` alone and inherited Npgsql for it — the csproj comment said the fix was to move the validator rather than copy it, and that's what happened. `cordango`'s output directory now contains no driver.

**The rename is complete**: `cordango` binary, `cordango.yaml`, `*.cordango.yaml`, `.cordango/`. Old names still read, and `fmt` migrates a pre-rename workspace and deletes what it replaced. That last part needed a fix I didn't anticipate — the content is byte-identical, so a content-comparing formatter reported a legacy workspace as "already canonical" and walked away. Five regression tests pin it. Token prefixes `cord_pat`/`cord_cxt` did **not** rename; they're a wire format shared with the server and with secret scanners.

## Two things the work found

The new `OssBoundaryTests` caught a transitional `InternalsVisibleTo` I'd left in `Cordango.AccessTokens` naming the platform — exactly the one-line reverse dependency that resolves perfectly from inside this working copy and breaks only in a public clone.

More interestingly: because `Corpus.RepoRoot()` now resolves the *Cordango* root, two tests started silently writing into the public checkout on every run. `CordOpsTests` regenerates the three Cord operation schemas for review (now `oss/cordango/schemas/ops/`), and `CordHandAuthoredAppsTests` writes round-trip artifacts (still private, now via a local `PlatformRoot()`). Worth remembering as a class of bug: after this split, anything anchored on "the repo root" is ambiguous.

## Verification

`dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` passes **1,135 tests from a copy outside your repo tree entirely** — no parent, no `backend/`, no database, no containers. The platform is at baseline: 3,548 tests versus 3,540 before, the difference being the 3 boundary and 5 legacy-name tests I added. The 125 API and 30 Runtime failures are the pre-existing DB-backed set; Docker Desktop isn't running, so I couldn't clear those — worth running `docker compose up -d db` and re-running before you commit.

## What needs you

Nothing is committed — that's four repositories (three submodules plus the parent pointer bump), and they're yours. Everything is staged. `docker-compose.yml` gained `./oss:/app/oss` on api and worker; the schema is an embedded resource, so without that mount those containers fail to *build*, naming a missing `.json` rather than a missing mount. They need a restart when you're ready.

The plan file is updated with your eight corrections folded in, and slices **S4–S10 — the standalone generator itself** — are untouched and ready. That's genuinely new construction rather than restructuring, so it seemed the right place to hand back.

"""Tim's call: permission semantics stay private, and a one-file assembly is not worth a project.

  Cordango.Authorization  -> back into backend/AppBuilder.Runtime (namespace AppBuilder.Runtime)
  Cordango.AccessTokens   -> folded into Cordango.Compiler/Tokens (namespace unchanged)
"""
import io, os, re, glob, shutil

SEP = chr(92)


def norm(p):
    return p.replace(SEP, '/')


def read(p):
    return io.open(p, encoding='utf-8-sig').read()


def write(p, t):
    io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(t)


# --- 1. Authorization back to Runtime ------------------------------------------------------------
for name in ('PermissionEvaluator.cs', 'FieldProjection.cs'):
    src = os.path.join('oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Authorization', name)
    t = read(src)
    assert 'namespace Cordango.Authorization;' in t, name
    t = t.replace('namespace Cordango.Authorization;', 'namespace AppBuilder.Runtime;')
    write(os.path.join('backend/AppBuilder.Runtime', name), t)
    print('returned', name, '-> backend/AppBuilder.Runtime')

# Every consumer loses the using; the types are back in a namespace they already import or share.
dropped = []
for p in glob.glob('backend/**/*.cs', recursive=True) + glob.glob('oss/**/*.cs', recursive=True):
    n = norm(p)
    if '/obj/' in n or '/bin/' in n or '/Cordango.Authorization/' in n:
        continue
    t = read(p)
    if 'Cordango.Authorization' not in t:
        continue
    t2 = re.sub(r'^using Cordango\.Authorization;\r?\n', '', t, flags=re.M)
    t2 = t2.replace('Cordango.Authorization.', 'AppBuilder.Runtime.')
    if t2 != t:
        write(p, t2)
        dropped.append(n)
print('dropped the using from', len(dropped), 'files')

# --- 2. AccessTokens folded into the compiler ----------------------------------------------------
os.makedirs('oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Tokens', exist_ok=True)
shutil.copy2('oss/cordango/src/Cordango.AccessTokens/CordAccessToken.cs',

"""Stamp the licence header onto every source file in the open-source repositories.

Idempotent: a file that already carries the marker is left alone, so this can be re-run after any
slice that adds files. A shebang keeps the first line.
"""
import io, os, glob, sys

MARKER = 'SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0'

REPOS = {
    'oss/cordango': ('Cordango', 'https://github.com/cordango/cordango',
                     'the open application language and compiler'),
    'oss/web-controls': ('Cordango Web Controls', 'https://github.com/cordango/web-controls',
                         'the shared Vue controls for Cordango applications'),
    'oss/examples': ('Cordango Examples', 'https://github.com/cordango/examples',
                     'example Cordango applications'),
}

SLASH = ('.cs', '.js', '.mjs', '.ts', '.vue')
HASH = ('.py',)


def header(prefix, name, url, what):
    return [
        prefix + ' SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0',
        prefix + ' Copyright (c) Cordango and contributors.',
        prefix + ' Part of ' + name + ', ' + what + ': ' + url,
        prefix + ' Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See LICENSE in the repository root.',
    ]


def stamp(path, prefix, name, url, what):
    raw = io.open(path, encoding='utf-8-sig').read()
    if MARKER in raw[:600]:
        return False

    lines = raw.split('\n')
    at = 0
    # A shebang has to stay on line one or the file stops being executable.
    if lines and lines[0].startswith('#!'):
        at = 1
        # Keep an encoding declaration with its shebang; PEP 263 only reads the first two lines.
        if len(lines) > 1 and 'coding' in lines[1] and lines[1].lstrip().startswith('#'):
            at = 2

    block = header(prefix, name, url, what)
    # One blank line between the header and whatever the file already started with, unless the file
    # is empty or already blank there.
    if at < len(lines) and lines[at].strip() != '':
        block = block + ['']

    lines[at:at] = block
    io.open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write('\n'.join(lines))
    return True


total = 0
skipped = 0
for repo, (name, url, what) in REPOS.items():
    if not os.path.isdir(repo):
        continue
    count = 0
    for path in sorted(glob.glob(repo + '/**/*', recursive=True)):
        n = path.replace(chr(92), '/')
        if not os.path.isfile(path):
            continue
        if '/bin/' in n or '/obj/' in n or '/node_modules/' in n or '/.git/' in n:
            continue
        ext = os.path.splitext(path)[1]
        prefix = '//' if ext in SLASH else '#' if ext in HASH else None
        if prefix is None:
            continue
        if stamp(path, prefix, name, url, what):
            count += 1
        else:
            skipped += 1
    print('%-20s %d file(s) stamped' % (repo, count))
    total += count

print()
print('total', total, 'stamped,', skipped, 'already had it')

implementation there means two sets of rules that agree until they quietly stop. Decide it then,
with the generator actually in front of us, rather than pre-emptively.

format moved into `Cordango.Compiler/Tokens/`. The reason it could not simply live in the CLI is

attachment.snippet:
1	# Cordango OSS split + standalone source generator
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	Tim's architecture document establishes the next product direction: alongside the existing platform, an open-source toolchain that takes a compiled App Definition JSON and **generates a complete, conventional, standalone application** (ASP.NET Core + EF Core + PostgreSQL + Vue 3 + Vuetify) that the user owns and deploys anywhere. The OSS/commercial boundary: OSS builds **one app** (auth, permissions, local Organizations/People/Departments/Groups, commands, processes, workflows, deterministic seeds); the platform keeps multi-app, cross-app, audit/history, AI, enrichment, platform search, marketplace, managed ops.
6	
7	Three GitHub repos **already exist** (private until launch): `https://github.com/cordango/cordango` (OSS monorepo), `https://github.com/cordango/web-controls` (`@cordango/web-controls`), `https://github.com/cordango/examples`. They get mounted into AppBuilder as **git submodules** so all work happens here but is committed to the separate repos from day one — the separation is physical, not aspirational.
8	
9	Branch: `CLI-CodeGen` (freshly cut from main, no work started).
10	
11	## Decisions locked with Tim
12	
13	1. **Submodules now** at `oss/cordango`, `oss/web-controls`, `oss/examples` (umbrella avoids the root `examples/` clash; one compose mount covers all three).
14	2. **Existing portable core moves now**: Definition + Cord + AccessTokens + Cli leave `backend/`, renamed `AppBuilder.*` → `Cordango.*`, into Tim's specified monorepo tree.
15	3. **CLI binary renames `cord` → `cordango` now**, **and the workspace format renames too**: `cord.yaml` → `cordango.yaml`, `.cord.yaml` → `.cordango.yaml`, `.cord/` → `.cordango/` (one-time legacy reads; zero external users make this the last cheap moment). Token prefixes `cord_pat`/`cord_cxt` do NOT rename (server wire format, issued tokens).
16	4. **Both run tracks live**: `cordango run` (local interpreted platform simulation, CordyOSS §7 packaged-Postgres track, for platform users) stays on the roadmap, **not scheduled here** and not blocked by anything here. This plan builds the standalone generator track.
17	5. **Tier-B UI blocks** (timeline, gantt, scheduling, planning, orgchart, intake, embeds): v1 rejects with CORD2111; `--allow-partial-ui` demotes to warning + visible "not supported" card **and a permanent scar in build metadata** (below).

content.text:
All four are done, everything green, and both repositories are staged.

**Authorization is reverted.** `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` are back in `AppBuilder.Runtime` and the `Cordango.Authorization` project is gone. I want to be straight about what that leaves open rather than let it disappear: the standalone scaffold still has to enforce permissions, and the reason I extracted it was to avoid two implementations that agree until they quietly stop. That problem is now deferred to S6, not solved. I've written it into the plan and the memory as an explicit decision point with three options to weigh when the generator is actually in front of us — generate the rules as *data* from the definition so there's no shared code at all, publish just the evaluator at that point, or accept a scaffold-local implementation pinned by shared fixtures. The first of those may well be better than what I built, since the definition already carries the grants.

**AccessTokens is no longer a project.** The single file moved to `Cordango.Compiler/Tokens/`. The one thing I kept from the old project's reasoning is in the csproj comment: it can't just live in the CLI, because a server writes the credential and the CLI reads it, and two implementations of that encoding drift at the checksum first and the hash second — neither of which surfaces as an error, only as tokens that verify on one side.

import io
p = r'C:\Users\timca\.claude\plans\heres-a-pretty-extensive-glimmering-lobster.md'

│   ├── Cordango.Authorization/     # PURE permission semantics: PermissionEvaluator + FieldProjection
│   │                               # moved from Runtime; platform Runtime and standalone BOTH wrap it
│   ├── Cordango.AccessTokens/      # one file; Api + Cli share it
│   ├── Cordango.Cli/               # AssemblyName=cordango"""
new = """│   │   ├── Semantics/   (ns Cordango.Semantics: ConditionEvaluator, TemplateResolver)
│   │   └── Tokens/      (ns Cordango.AccessTokens: the credential format a server writes
│   │                     and the CLI reads — no assembly of its own)
│   ├── Cordango.Cli/               # AssemblyName=cordango"""
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)

old2 = """scaffold-instantiation test: materialize → `dotnet build` + `npm ci && npm run build` green; authorization tests exercise the **shared** `Cordango.Authorization` component through the scaffold adapter."""
new2 = """scaffold-instantiation test: materialize → `dotnet build` + `npm ci && npm run build` green; authorization is the scaffold's OWN code, checked against the shared decision fixtures (below)."""
assert old2 in t
t = t.replace(old2, new2)

old3 = """- **Permission semantics stay PRIVATE.** `Cordango.Authorization` was built and then reverted;
  `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` are back in `AppBuilder.Runtime`. The problem it solved
  is unresolved and returns at **S6**: the standalone scaffold needs permission enforcement, and a
  second implementation means two sets of rules that agree until they quietly stop. Options to weigh
  then: generate the rules as data from the definition (no shared code at all), publish only the
  evaluator at that point, or accept a scaffold-local implementation pinned by shared fixtures."""
new3 = """- **Standalone security is DELIBERATELY SEPARATE, and this is now settled rather than deferred.**
  Two things were conflated and they need separating:

  **Authentication** — who the caller is: login, sessions, password hashing, tokens. Stock ASP.NET
  Core Identity (plus OpenIddict only if a generated app ever needs to be an OAuth server, which v1
  does not). None of the platform's authentication was ever going to be shared, and none should be.
  Nothing to decide.

  **Authorization** — what the definition's `roles[]` mean: union across roles, specific grant beats
  `*`, field override else role default, commands deny-by-default. I argued this belonged in a
  shared component and I was wrong about the framing. It is not security infrastructure, it is
  definition interpretation, in the same family as computed expressions and conditions. But sharing
  it still creates the thing Tim is right to refuse: a coupling where a change made for standalone
  reasons alters platform enforcement. Blast radius, not secrecy.

  **So: the scaffold gets its OWN permission code, and drift is DETECTED rather than prevented.**
  A conformance fixture — `tests/fixtures/permissions/*.json`, a list of
  `(definition, roles, entity, field, operation) → expected decision` — is generated once from the
  platform evaluator, checked into the public repo as DATA, and asserted by both the platform suite
  and the generated app's own suite. No shared assembly, no coupling, and a divergence becomes a red
  test instead of a wrong answer in production. Cheap: the rules are small and finite.

  `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` stay in `AppBuilder.Runtime` and are not published."""
assert old3 in t
t = t.replace(old3, new3)
io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(t)

4

12	
13	1. **Submodules now** at `oss/cordango`, `oss/web-controls`, `oss/examples` (umbrella avoids the root `examples/` clash; one compose mount covers all three).
14	2. **Existing portable core moves now**: Definition + Cord + AccessTokens + Cli leave `backend/`, renamed `AppBuilder.*` → `Cordango.*`, into Tim's specified monorepo tree.
15	3. **CLI binary renames `cord` → `cordango` now**, **and the workspace format renames too**: `cord.yaml` → `cordango.yaml`, `.cord.yaml` → `.cordango.yaml`, `.cord/` → `.cordango/` (one-time legacy reads; zero external users make this the last cheap moment). Token prefixes `cord_pat`/`cord_cxt` do NOT rename (server wire format, issued tokens).
16	4. **Both run tracks live**: `cordango run` (local interpreted platform simulation, CordyOSS §7 packaged-Postgres track, for platform users) stays on the roadmap, **not scheduled here** and not blocked by anything here. This plan builds the standalone generator track.

20	8. **EF/backend generation follows Tim's TCDev.APIGenerator pattern** (DeeJayTC/net-dynamic-api): generic scaffold machinery + thin generated per-entity types, EF-native automated migrations. Details below; S6 opens with a reuse assessment of the APIGenerator codebase itself.

23

26	
27	  **Authentication** — who the caller is: login, sessions, password hashing, tokens. Stock ASP.NET
28	  Core Identity (plus OpenIddict only if a generated app ever needs to be an OAuth server, which v1
29	  does not). None of the platform's authentication was ever going to be shared, and none should be.
30	  Nothing to decide.
31	
32	  **Authorization** — what the definition's `roles[]` mean: union across roles, specific grant beats
33	  `*`, field override else role default, commands deny-by-default. I argued this belonged in a
34	  shared component and I was wrong about the framing. It is not security infrastructure, it is
35	  definition interpretation, in the same family as computed expressions and conditions. But sharing
36	  it still creates the thing Tim is right to refuse: a coupling where a change made for standalone
37	  reasons alters platform enforcement. Blast radius, not secrecy.
38	
39	  **So: the scaffold gets its OWN permission code, and drift is DETECTED rather than prevented.**
40	  A conformance fixture — `tests/fixtures/permissions/*.json`, a list of
41	  `(definition, roles, entity, field, operation) → expected decision` — is generated once from the
42	  platform evaluator, checked into the public repo as DATA, and asserted by both the platform suite
43	  and the generated app's own suite. No shared assembly, no coupling, and a divergence becomes a red
44	  test instead of a wrong answer in production. Cheap: the rules are small and finite.
45	
46	  `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` stay in `AppBuilder.Runtime` and are not published.
47	- **No one-file assemblies.** `Cordango.AccessTokens` folded into `Cordango.Compiler/Tokens/`. The
48	  format still cannot live in the CLI alone — a server writes it and the CLI reads it.
49	- **`samples/` → `tests/corpus/`.** `cordango/examples` is the examples repository; the compiler's

content.text:
Your instinct was right, and I was wrong about the framing — but I want to separate two things I'd bundled, because only one of them was ever a real question.

**Authentication was never on the table.** Login, sessions, password hashing, tokens — the scaffold was always going to be stock ASP.NET Core Identity with a cookie for the same-origin SPA. Nothing of the platform's authentication was going to be shared, and nothing should be. That part of your message needs no argument from me; it's what the plan already said.

**Authorization is where I over-reached.** What I extracted wasn't security infrastructure — it was the interpretation of `roles[]`: union across roles, specific grant beats `*`, field override else role default, commands deny-by-default. That's the same family of thing as a computed expression or a condition, which is why I reached for the same "one implementation" argument I'd used for `ConditionEvaluator`. Calling it "the permission semantics" made it sound like I was proposing to share auth, which I wasn't, and that's on me.

But your conclusion holds anyway, for a reason I under-weighted. The problem with a shared assembly isn't secrecy — publishing 161 lines that read a JSON array doesn't weaken anything, and `Gate.cs` already validates those same structures in public. The problem is **blast radius**: once the platform and a generated app link the same library, a change made for standalone reasons can alter platform enforcement. Deliberately separate is the right call, and it's the right call for that reason rather than the one I'd have given.

So the drift risk I raised is real but it doesn't need shared code to answer — it needs to be **detected rather than prevented**. The scaffold gets its own permission code, and a conformance fixture — a list of `(definition, roles, entity, field, operation) → expected decision`, generated once from the platform evaluator and checked into the public repo as plain data — gets asserted by both the platform suite and the generated app's own suite. No assembly in common, no coupling, and a divergence shows up as a red test instead of a wrong answer in production. The rules are small and finite, so the fixture is cheap.

That's now settled in the plan, STATUS.md and memory rather than left as an open S6 question, so it doesn't get relitigated when the scaffold gets built. `PermissionEvaluator` and `FieldProjection` stay in `AppBuilder.Runtime`, unpublished. I also cleaned up two stale references to the reverted project that had survived in the plan's target tree and its S6 acceptance criteria.

Nothing to rebuild — the revert already landed and everything is still green (1,302 OSS, platform at baseline). All four repos remain staged for you.

new = """## Latest (2026-08-20 — GENERATOR SDK: the capability gate, before any generator exists ✅)

`cordango check --target standalone` now answers whether an application can be built as a standalone
project, and names every reason it cannot. No generator emits source yet — that is deliberate. A
target is two separable things, a CLAIM about what it can build and the code that builds it, and
publishing the claim first means the capability list is written from the language rather than
backwards from whatever the emitters happened to manage.

**New: `Cordango.SourceGen`** (the SDK: `CompiledAppArtifact`, `IAppSourceGenerator`,
`GeneratorCapabilities`, `TargetValidator`, `GeneratedFileWriter`, `BuildMetadata`) and
`Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue` (capabilities only; `Generate` refuses honestly rather than answering
"no files" and writing an empty directory that claims success). Plus `cordango targets`,
`--target` on `check`, and `validate` as the spelling people reach for when asking about a target.

**The measured answer, pinned as a table** (`tests/Compatibility.Tests`, over the same 15-app corpus
the gate uses). Eight applications build with no refusals at all. **Five are blocked only by
screens** — helpdesk (intake, answers), people-hr (orgchart), sales-crm (widgets), task-manager
(gantt), time-off (timeline) — meaning their entities, processes, commands, workflows and
permissions are all supported and `--allow-partial-ui` is enough to ship them. **Two are refused on
architecture**: ventures places an audit block, and budget-planner adds an ordered series, `prev()`
and windowed rollups. Set equality, not "contains", so widening a capability has to be an edit to
that table.

**Two real defects came out of writing the tests, which is the point of writing them.** The block
walker originally covered `pages` and `views` — the obvious places screens live — and missed every
block on an entity's own `detail`, so it reported ventures and task-manager as buildable when they
are not (ventures' audit block sits at `$.entities[0].detail.blocks[4].columns[1][0].tabs[4].blocks[0]`).
It now walks the whole document with one exact exclusion: elements of the top-level `entities` array,
because an entity's `kind` collides with the `settings` block. And the writer normalised line endings
at WRITE time while the metadata hashed the content as supplied, so a generator emitting `\\r\\n`
produced byte-identical files and a different manifest from one emitting `\\n` — the determinism claim
failing inside the artifact that documents it.

**Capabilities carry reasons, not booleans**, and a test enforces it: every block kind, effect,
trigger and field type the schema allows is either supported or withheld WITH a sentence, so adding
to the language forces the choice to be made rather than defaulting to a silent "unsupported". Same
doctrine as `CordWordMap.Withheld` in the Cord vocabulary. `cordango targets` prints both halves.

**The writer owns the filesystem** so a generator cannot escape the output directory, cannot leave
half a tree behind, and cannot make two runs differ by iterating a dictionary. Regeneration deletes
exactly the files the previous `cordango.build.json` lists and nothing else, and a non-empty
directory without that manifest is refused rather than merged into. 20 determinism tests, including
generating the same tree twice from differently-ordered inputs and comparing hashes.

OSS repo now at **1,366 tests**, still green from a clone with no platform above it. Platform
unchanged at baseline.

"""
assert anchor in t
io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(t.replace(anchor, new + anchor, 1))
print('STATUS.md updated')
PYEOF

content.text:
S4 is done. The capability gate ships before any generator, which turned out to be the right order: writing its tests found two real defects and produced a compatibility answer that differs from what the plan assumed.

**What works now.** `cordango check --target standalone` (and `validate`, the word people reach for when asking about a target) answers whether an app can be built standalone and names every reason it can't, with a CORD21xx code and a JSON path. `cordango targets` prints what each target builds *and what it deliberately won't, with the reason* — capabilities carry sentences rather than booleans, and a test enforces that every block kind, effect, trigger and field type the schema allows is classified one way or the other. That's the same `CordWordMap.Withheld` doctrine that exists because an agent couldn't tell a gap from a decision.

`DotNetVueGenerator` declares its capabilities but refuses to generate, honestly — returning "no files" would have produced an empty directory and a build manifest claiming everything went fine.

**The measured compatibility table, which beat my estimate.** Over the same 15-app corpus:

- **8 build clean**: expenses, finance, invoicing, payroll, recruiting, room-booking, timesheets, crm
- **5 are blocked only by screens**: helpdesk (intake, answers), people-hr (orgchart), sales-crm (widgets), task-manager (gantt), time-off (timeline). Their entities, processes, commands, workflows and permissions are all supported, so `--allow-partial-ui` is enough to ship them.
- **2 refuse on architecture**: ventures (audit block), budget-planner (audit + series + `prev()` + windowed rollups)

The plan predicted roughly this shape but named the wrong apps and undercounted. It matters for sequencing: **a third of the corpus needs `--allow-partial-ui`**, so the tier-B emitters are worth more at S9 than I'd assumed. That's recorded in the plan.

**Two defects the tests found.** The block walker originally covered `pages` and `views` — the obvious places screens live — and missed every block on an entity's own `detail`. Ventures' audit block sits at `$.entities[0].detail.blocks[4].columns[1][0].tabs[4].blocks[0]`, so the gate said "buildable" about an app that isn't. It now walks the whole document with one exact exclusion: elements of the top-level `entities` array, because an entity's `kind` collides with the `settings` block. Second, the writer normalised line endings at write time while the metadata hashed the content as supplied — so a generator emitting `\r\n` produced byte-identical files and a *different manifest* from one emitting `\n`. The determinism claim failing inside the artifact that documents it.

**The writer owns the filesystem**, which is why a generator is handed no directory: it can't escape the output root, can't leave half a tree behind, and can't make two runs differ by iterating a dictionary. Regeneration deletes exactly what the previous `cordango.build.json` lists and nothing else; a non-empty directory without that manifest is refused rather than merged into. A partial build scars the metadata permanently, per your earlier note.

OSS repo is at **1,366 tests**, verified green from a clone with no platform above it. Platform unchanged at baseline (125 API tests still waiting on Postgres). Everything staged across all four repos.

content.text:
Let me answer the audit-block question first, since it's the one where the existing decision was yours.

The `history` block is the one screen fed entirely by the platform's audit subsystem — you place `kind: history` and the runtime fills it from `FieldHistoryStore` (every field change, before and after, with actor and timestamp) plus `AppEventStore`. No entity, no fields, no authoring. Your architecture doc §21 excluded it from standalone by name ("record history, field history, business activity feeds, before/after history"), and §22 said an audit-dependent block should be *rejected* rather than silently dropped, which is where CORD2102 came from. So that exclusion is yours, not mine — but it's a commercial boundary, not a technical one. The implementation is cheap: it's the before-image the write path already computes, kept instead of discarded.

The other two I'll flip now, because you're right on both.

content.text: All 15 corpus apps now build standalone, and the refusal codes moved to synthetic fixtures so every code is still covered. Two decisions I'd rather not make for you:

questions.question: I've provisionally made the `history` block supported, which reverses §21 of your architecture doc ("Standalone applications should not receive Cordango's audit system — record history, field history, before/after history"). Technically it's cheap: the write path already computes the before-image, so it's a table plus keeping what it currently discards. Commercially it's a boundary you drew deliberately. Keep it in?

options.label: Keep it in standalone (Recommended)
options.description: A single app's own record history is table stakes for a business app, and the platform's audit VALUE is the cross-app part — governance, company-wide activity trails, the audit explorer across many apps — which standalone still won't have. Costs one table plus retaining the before-image. Ventures and Budget Planner then build with zero refusals.

options.label: Keep it platform-only, per §21
options.description: Restore CORD2102. Standalone gets technical logs only; ventures and budget-planner each report one refusal for their history blocks. Audit stays a visible reason to be on the platform. I revert the capability and the compatibility table records both apps as refused.

options.label: In, but write-only for now
options.description: Generate the history table and record changes into it from day one, but don't emit the history SCREEN yet (CORD2111 rather than CORD2102). Keeps the data so nothing is lost, defers the UI to the same slice as the other tier-B screens.

questions.question: With series/prev()/windowed rollups now in scope, the recompute cascade is the single hardest thing in the generator — it took two passes to make fast on the platform (edit >180s→1.5s, grid 12min→67s). What order do you want the remaining slices in?

options.label: Prove the cascade first (Recommended)
options.description: Jump to the computed/recompute engine before the scaffold and emitters: build it against Budget Planner as the acceptance case, in isolation, with unit tests. If the design is wrong we find out now rather than after building a scaffold and backend around it. Then return to the plan order (controls → scaffold → backend → Vue).

options.label: Follow the plan order
options.description: S5 web-controls next (extract the zero-edit modules and seam-cut components), then S6 scaffold, S7 backend emitters, S8 workflows/computed, S9 Vue. Steady progression, each slice independently verifiable; the cascade risk is carried until S8.

options.label: Scaffold first
options.description: S6 next — the standalone app skeleton (Identity auth, generic controller/DbContext, org module, docker), which makes the first runnable generated app the nearest milestone. The cascade and the controls both come after.

content.text:
Both corrections are in, all green (1,377 OSS, platform at baseline).

**On the audit block** — it's the one screen fed entirely by the platform's audit subsystem: you write `kind: history` and the runtime fills it from a field-level change log (what changed, who, before and after). Your §21 drew that line, so it stays platform-only, and the refusal now reads as an offer rather than a wall:

> `CORD2102: 'history' block: record history is a Cordango Platform feature. The platform keeps a field-level audit trail for every record automatically (what changed, who changed it, and the value before and after), and this block is the screen that shows it. A standalone application keeps technical logs but no business audit trail, so there is nothing behind the block to render. Remove the block to build standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform, where the trail is kept for you with nothing to configure.`

A test pins that wording — it must name the platform, say what the trail gives you, and offer both ways out. A refusal that reads as "unsupported" turns a sales conversation into a bug report. I also stripped the em-dashes I'd put in it, since it's user-facing copy.

Worth noting the two remaining refusals are different in kind, and the messages now say so: `relatedApps` is a question with *no answer* when there's one application, while history is a capability someone can choose to have. Only the second is an upsell.

**On scope** — you were right and my first pass had the method backwards. I declared the target from what would be easy to emit, then measured. That produced a boundary where the flagship Budget Planner couldn't be built, which is absurd for a target meant to demonstrate the calculation plane. Scope now comes from the language: every screen is in (gantt, timeline, orgchart, intake, answers, embeds, widgets) and so is the whole calculation plane (ordered series, `prev()`, windowed and matched rollups). What's out is exactly what needs *other applications* or *a model* — cross-app references, `relatedApps`, `enrich`, and history. That line explains itself in one sentence, which the old one couldn't.

All 15 corpus apps build now; ventures and budget-planner stop at the audit block and nothing else.

**One consequence you should have in view.** Bringing series and windowed rollups in makes S8 the big slice: the expressions were already shared, so what's newly committed is the *recompute cascade* — working out which records a write disturbs and in what order. That's the piece that took two passes to make fast on the platform. Your instruction that it must come out as generic deterministic generated code rather than a hand-tuned engine is recorded as the constraint on that slice, with Budget Planner as the acceptance case.

Next is **S5, the web-controls extraction** — the zero-edit pure modules (`manifest.js`, `blockspec/`, `formatting.js`, `responsive.js`, the table composables) plus the seam-cut components (`CordangoDataTable`, `FieldInput`, `KanbanCore`, `ChartCard`, the pickers). Now that every screen is in scope, that extraction has to cover the timeline, gantt and calendar machinery too rather than stopping at tier A.

All four platform-only refusals now read the same way, and a test enforces the shape rather than leaving it to whoever edits the capability list next: name the feature as a Cordango Platform capability, say what the platform does with it, say what a standalone build carries instead, and give both ways forward.

`relatedApps` now reads:

> **related apps is a Cordango Platform feature.** On the platform every application shares one set of People and Organizations, so this block can show the deals, tickets and projects from across the company that point at this record. A standalone application has its own local People and Organizations and nothing installed beside it, so there is nothing for the block to look through. Remove the block to build standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform.

I did the same for the `enrich` effect and for cross-app references, which had been the weakest of the four — it previously ended on "cross-application references are what the platform is for", which is a shrug rather than an offer. Here's what a user actually gets now:

```
CORD2100: 'task.customer' points at 'crm', a separately installed application: references
between applications are a Cordango Platform feature. The platform runs several applications
on one shared company graph, so a record in one can point at a record in another. A standalone
build is a single application: it carries its own People, Organizations, Departments and Groups
and can reference those, but there is no second application for this field to resolve against.
Point the field at a local entity to build standalone, or run this application on Cordango
Platform.  ($.entities[0].fields[4])
```

Two things I dropped along the way. The "two different kinds of refusal" distinction I'd built into the code comments and the test structure is gone — you were right that it's a distinction that matters to an architect and not to the person reading the error, and keeping it would have meant the messages drifting apart again later. And three messages were joining their context to their explanation with a period, so the reason started a sentence in lowercase; they all use a colon now, which is what the block and effect messages already did.

Verified end to end through the CLI on a scratch workspace, not just in tests. OSS repo at **1,382 tests** green, platform unchanged at baseline. Staged across all four repos.

Next is S5, the web-controls extraction — and with every screen now in scope, that has to cover the timeline, gantt, calendar and org-chart machinery rather than stopping at the tier-A components I'd originally listed.

You may have meant move them out entirely — and they can't go, because `dotnet test Cordango.slnx` has to pass from a standalone clone and the whole suite is pinned to those files. The corpus and the examples are different things: one is test fixtures that must not drift, the other is a showcase that should. The examples repo needs its own curated copies, which is what's missing.

import io, os

TOP = """# Cordango examples

Four complete Cordango applications, as source you can clone, read, change and build.

> Status: pre-alpha. These track the App Definition schema in
> [cordango/cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango) and will move while it settles.

Each directory is a real workspace, not a snippet. What you see is what an author writes: one file
per aggregate, an entity here, a lifecycle there, a role, a screen. There is no compiled artifact
checked in, because a compiled App Definition is the output of the toolchain rather than the thing a
person edits.

```
cd expenses
cordango check                              # parse, lower and validate. No model, no database.
cordango inspect                            # what is in here
cordango check --target standalone          # can this be generated as an app you own?
```

## The examples

| Example | Entities | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`expenses/`](expenses) | 1 | The smallest complete application, and the one to read first. An approval lifecycle, three roles that see different things, and a claim that only its owner may edit. |
| [`time-off/`](time-off) | 1 | Absence requests with a manager approval step, a team schedule, and dates that mean something (a request knows how many working days it spans). |
| [`task-manager/`](task-manager) | 5 | Projects, tasks, subtasks and milestones, with rollups that count a parent's children. The one to read for computed fields. |
| [`room-booking/`](room-booking) | 4 | Rooms, bookings, attendees and a policy entity that configures the rules. Shows a configuration entity and a calendar. |

## Reading one

Start with `apps/<name>/app.cordango.yaml`, which names the application and the order things appear
in. Then:

```
entities/          what the application stores, one file per entity
workflows/         lifecycles (a record's states and the moves between them) and automations
roles/             who may read, write and run what
views/collections/ a table, board or calendar over one entity
views/screens/     a page, assembled from views and blocks
views/entities/    a single record's detail, peek and form
```

## Contributing

An improvement here benefits everyone using the example, in either environment. Useful contributions
include clearer labels, more realistic permissions, a state a lifecycle is missing, and screens that
read better.

Two things to check before opening a pull request:

```
cordango check --app <name>
cordango check --app <name> --target standalone
```

The first asks whether it is a valid Cordango application. The second asks whether the standalone
generator can also build it, which is a narrower question: a standalone build is one application, so
anything that depends on other installed applications is reported rather than silently dropped.

## Where these came from

Each one was imported from the conformance corpus in the compiler repository with
`cordango import`, which turns an App Definition back into source. That corpus stays where it is
because the test suite is pinned to it and must not drift. These copies are the ones meant for
people, and they are allowed to grow.

## License

Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
"""

io.open('oss/examples/README.md', 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(TOP)
print('top-level README written')

EXAMPLES = {
 'expenses': ("Expenses", """An employee files an expense claim. An approver either approves it or declines it, and once it is
approved somebody marks it reimbursed.

It is the smallest application here that is still complete, which makes it the one to read first.

## What to look at

**`workflows/lifecycles/claim_flow.cordango.yaml`** is the heart of it. Four states, the moves
between them, and which of those moves is allowed from where. `submitted` is where a claim starts,
`reimbursed` and `declined` are terminal, and there is no path back out of either. The states carry
colours because the renderer uses them, so a declined claim looks declined without anybody writing a
condition.

**`roles/`** has three files and they are not variations on one theme. An employee sees their own
claims. An approver sees the queue. An admin sees everything and can change the categories. Read
them together: the difference between them is the application's security model, and it is enforced
by the server rather than by which screen you happen to be on.

**`views/screens/`** has three pages over one entity, which is the point. The same claims appear as
"my expenses" to the person who filed them and as an inbox to the person approving them.

## Running it

```
cordango check
cordango check --target standalone
```
"""),
 'time-off': ("Time off", """Somebody requests time off. Their manager approves it. The team schedule shows who is away.

## What to look at

**`entities/time_off.cordango.yaml`** for dates that carry meaning. A request knows the day it
starts, the day it ends and how many working days that spans, and the last of those is computed
rather than typed. Nobody has to remember to update it, and nobody can get it wrong.

**`workflows/lifecycles/approval.cordango.yaml`** is deliberately shorter than the expenses one.
Approval is two states and a decision, and an application that models it with six is describing the
software rather than the business.

**`views/screens/schedule.cordango.yaml`** is the calendar. It reads the same records the approval
queue does, presented against a date axis instead of a list.

## Running it

```
cordango check
cordango check --target standalone
```
"""),
 'task-manager': ("Task manager", """Projects hold tasks. Tasks hold subtasks and comments. Milestones group work by date.

Five entities, which makes this the one to read for how records relate to each other and how a
parent learns about its children.

## What to look at

**`entities/project.cordango.yaml`** and **`entities/task.cordango.yaml`** together. A project does
not store how many tasks are open; it computes it, by rolling up the tasks that point at it. Change
a task and the project's count follows, because the relationship is declared rather than maintained.

**`entities/task_section.cordango.yaml`** is a task's own subtasks: the same entity pointing at
itself, which is how a checklist inside a task works without a second concept.

**`views/screens/projects.cordango.yaml`** is the largest screen in these examples. Read it after
the smaller ones.

## Running it

```
cordango check
cordango check --target standalone
```
"""),
 'room-booking': ("Room booking", """Rooms get booked. Bookings have attendees. A policy entity decides the rules.

## What to look at

**`entities/booking_policy.cordango.yaml`** is a configuration entity, and it is the reason to read
this example. How far ahead people may book, whether approval is needed, how long a booking may run:
those are settings a company changes, so they are rows in a table rather than constants in the
source. An application that hard-codes them needs a developer every time somebody changes their
mind.

**`entities/booking_attendee.cordango.yaml`** is the join between a booking and the people on it,
which is what a many-to-many relationship looks like when it has its own fields.

**`views/screens/availability.cordango.yaml`** is a calendar over rooms rather than over people.

## Running it

```
cordango check
cordango check --target standalone
```
"""),
}

for name, (title, body) in EXAMPLES.items():

```
cordango.yaml            the workspace: which apps are installed
apps/""" + name + """/
  app.cordango.yaml      the application's name, and the order things appear in
  entities/              what it stores
  workflows/             lifecycles and automations
  roles/                 who may do what
  views/                 collections, screens, and one record's detail
```
"""
    io.open(os.path.join('oss/examples', name, 'README.md'), 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(text)
    print('wrote', name + '/README.md')

# Cordango examples

Complete Cordango application definitions you can read, generate, run and change.

> Status: pre-alpha. Definitions here track the App Definition schema in
> [cordango/cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango) and will move while that schema settles.

```
cordango build --app expenses --target standalone --out ./expenses-app
cd expenses-app

```

or install it into Cordango Platform, where it shares people, organizations and permissions with
every other app in the company.

cordango check --app <name> --target standalone
```

The first asks whether the definition is a valid Cordango application. The second asks whether it is
also compatible with the standalone generator, which supports less than the platform does and says
exactly what it cannot do.

## Relationship to the compiler repository

`cordango/cordango` carries its own `samples/` directory. That one is the conformance corpus: it is
pinned by the test suite and changes only when the contract does. This repository is the one meant
for people, and it is allowed to grow, improve and diverge.

# Task manager

open_tasks:

both milestones settle, because the relationship is declared rather than maintained.

a second concept for it.

# Time off

Somebody requests time off. Their manager approves or declines it. A calendar shows who is away.

One entity, three roles, three screens. Read it after `expenses` to see how differently the same
shape can be presented.

## What to look at

**`views/screens/schedule.cordango.yaml`** is the interesting file, and the reason to read this one.
It is a calendar, and a calendar needs to know which month it is showing:

```yaml
screen: schedule
label: Who's off
state:
  - key: cursor
    type: date
    default: '{{today}}'
```

That `state` block is screen state. The cursor belongs to the page rather than to any record, it
starts at today, and moving it is what pages the calendar back and forth. It is the mechanism behind
every screen that has a position of its own, and this is the smallest example of it.

**`workflows/lifecycles/approval.cordango.yaml`** is deliberately shorter than the expenses one.
Approval is a decision with two outcomes, and modelling it with six states would describe the
software rather than the business.

**`roles/`** shows the same three-way split as `expenses` over completely different subject matter,
which is worth comparing: an employee sees their own requests, a manager sees the queue, an admin
sees everything.

new = """## Latest (2026-08-20 — `cordango import`, and the examples repository is no longer empty ✅)

Tim asked where the examples went. Nothing was lost: the old samples all moved into
`oss/cordango/tests/corpus/` (13 reference apps, crm, budget-planner, the 200-file CordSource
specimen) and `tests/fixtures/` (historical, interactive, invalid, raw-allowlist). Those stay put
because `dotnet test Cordango.slnx` is pinned to them and has to pass from a standalone clone. What
was genuinely missing is the examples repository, whose README I had written in S0 listing four
examples that did not exist.

**New command: `cordango import <app.definition.json>`.** It is the missing half of `publish` —
publishing turned source into a definition and there was no way back, so an application that existed
as a definition could not be opened or edited as files at all, which is strange in a product whose
claim is that your application is source you own. It gates the document first (importing something
that was never valid produces a model whose wrongness the resulting source cannot explain), imports
into the semantic model, and writes it back through `CordSource` — so what lands is what an author
would have written, one file per aggregate, not a renamed copy of the input.

**`cordango/examples` now holds four workspaces**, produced with that command rather than by a
script, so they were made the way a user would make them: expenses (1 entity, the smallest complete
app), time-off (screen state, a calendar cursor), task-manager (5 entities, five rollups on
milestone), room-booking (a `kind: settings` policy record, a many-to-many with fields). Each is a
real workspace with `cordango.yaml` and `apps/<name>/**.cordango.yaml`, and all four report

**No compiled definition is checked in**, deliberately. An examples repository full of compiled JSON
teaches people the compiler's output rather than the language, and it would duplicate the corpus,
which is the thing that was objected to in the first place.

**The imported source came out cleaner than expected**: zero raw App Definition fragments across all
four, so nothing in them shows through as an unmodelled block tree. I had warned this would be
visible and it is not, for these four.

Every claim in the four READMEs was checked against the files rather than drafted from memory. One
draft asserted time-off computes a working-day duration; it does not, and that sentence is gone.

"""
assert anchor in t
io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(t.replace(anchor, new + anchor, 1))

content.text:
The examples repo is populated now, and the short answer to your question is that nothing was lost — it was never filled in. Seeding it was S10, the last slice, and the README I wrote in S0 listed four examples as if they already existed. That was the actual defect.

The old samples all moved into the compiler repo when you objected to `samples/` sitting next to an examples repository:

| Was | Now |
|---|---|
| `exploration/reference/*.appdef.json` (13 apps) | `oss/cordango/tests/corpus/reference/` |
| `schema/examples/crm.appdef.json` | `oss/cordango/tests/corpus/crm.appdef.json` |
| `exploration/budget-planner.appdef.json` | `oss/cordango/tests/corpus/budget-planner.appdef.json` |
| `examples/semantic/budgetPlanner/` (200 files) | `oss/cordango/tests/corpus/semantic/budgetPlanner/` |
| `schema/examples/tests/{generated,interactive}`, `invalid` | `oss/cordango/tests/fixtures/` |

I read your comment as being about the *name*, so I renamed to `tests/corpus/`. Those can't move out: `dotnet test Cordango.slnx` has to pass from a standalone clone and the whole suite is pinned to them. The corpus is fixtures that must not drift; the examples are a showcase that should. Different jobs, so both exist.

**`cordango import` is new**, and it's the missing half of `publish`. Publishing turned source into a definition with no way back, so an application that existed as a definition couldn't be opened or edited as files at all — odd in a product whose claim is that your app is source you own. It gates the document first, imports into the semantic model, then writes back through `CordSource`, so what lands is what an author would have written rather than a renamed copy of the input. I added it rather than scripting the conversion because a script would have been a second implementation of the same thing.

**The four examples are real workspaces**, `cordango.yaml` plus `apps/<name>/**.cordango.yaml`, made with that command so they were produced the way a user would produce them. All four report `ok, builds with dotnet-vue`. No compiled definition is checked in: that would teach people the compiler's output instead of the language, and duplicate the corpus again.

Two things worth flagging. The imported source came out **cleaner than I warned** — zero raw App Definition fragments across all four, so nothing shows through as an unmodelled block tree. And when I drafted the time-off README I claimed it computes a working-day duration; it doesn't, and I caught it by checking the file rather than shipping it. Every claim in the four READMEs is now verified against the source.

I picked what each README leads with from what's actually distinctive: milestone's five rollups in task-manager, the `kind: settings` policy record in room-booking, the calendar's `cursor` screen state in time-off, and the three genuinely different role files in expenses.

All three repos staged. Still to do from your earlier answer: nine more reference apps as examples "later", and S5 web-controls is next in the plan.

## `oss/web-controls` — `@cordango/web-controls` v1

- Vite library mode (ESM+cjs), `vue`/`vuetify`/`vue-i18n` as **peerDependencies**, `node --test` for pure modules, no Pinia. Install plugin `CordangoControls` with injected seams: `{ i18n, peopleDirectory, isMe, mediaUrl, tableSettings, commandInvoker }`.
- **Moves first**: pure modules (`manifest.js`, `i18n/formatting.js`, `responsive.js`, `filterMemory.js`, `views/{timeRange,dayGrid,weeklyHours,chipsEditor,companyGroup,inlineCreate}.js`, `tables/use*` + their tests) and seam-cut components: `ChartCard`→`CordangoChartCard` (already standalone), `UiDataTable`→`CordangoDataTable`, `FieldInput`→`CordangoFieldInput`, `KanbanCore`→`CordangoKanban`, `ProcessBlock`→`CordangoProcess`, `UiRefPicker`/Person* (directory injected), pure `Ui*` primitives. Each moved file notes its `web/` origin (drift greppable).
- **Stays out**: `data.js`/`commands.js`/`me.js` (REST shape belongs to the app), vue-router (deep links → emitted events), `blockspec/`, `BlockRenderer.vue`.
- **Consumption before npm publish**: generator emits `vendor/cordango-web-controls/` (built dist, `controlsVersion` in build metadata); generated `package.json` uses `"file:./vendor/cordango-web-controls"`. Self-contained, offline, deterministic. npm publish later flips one dependency line (vendoring stays as `--vendor-controls`).
- **Platform `web/` migration is NOT a prerequisite** and not scheduled here.

    if 'SPDX-License-Identifier' in t[:400]:
        continue
    rel = p.replace(os.sep, '/')
    origin = ORIGIN.get(rel) or 'web/src/' + rel[len('src/'):]
    note = ('// Extracted from the Cordango platform at ' + origin + '. Until web/ consumes this\n'

    io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(HDR + note + '\n' + t)
    n += 1

print('stamped', n, 'files with licence + provenance')
PYEOF

content.text:
S5's first half is done, and it turned up a live bug in the platform.

**The package now has real content**: seventeen modules, 151 tests, both bundle formats building. `manifest.js`, `filterMemory.js`, `responsive.js`, `formatting.js`, the six date-surface modules that sit behind timelines and calendars, and the five table composables. No components yet — those are the larger half and each needs its host seam cut individually.

The extraction was clean because every import in that set turned out to be either internal to the set or a peer dependency (`vue`, `vuetify`). Only `formatting.js` reached into the host, for `currentLocale()`. That's now `src/locale.js`, a settable source wired by the `CordangoControls` plugin, defaulting to English rather than `navigator.language` — a control that guessed the browser's language would pass every test on an English machine and render German dates on your laptop.

**Then the smoke test found something.** I formatted the same date under `en` and `de` and got identical output. The cause is in `manifest.js`:

```js
d.toLocaleDateString(undefined, { year: 'numeric', month: 'short', day: 'numeric' })
```

`undefined` reads as "use the default locale" and means "use the **browser's**". So a German workspace renders English dates for anyone whose browser is set to English, and the reverse. It's the exact rule your 2026-08-08 localisation work established — `toLocale*` forbidden, everything through `i18n/formatting.js` — and about 30 sites were converted then. **31 were missed and are still live in `web/src`:**

| File | Sites |
|---|---|
| `manifest.js` | 7 |
| `home/widgets.js` | 6 |
| `home/HomeWidgetCard.vue` | 2 |
| `public/BookingPage.vue` | 2 |
| `blockAggregate.js` | 1 |
| others across views | 13 |

`manifest.js` even carries a comment describing its formatters as "locale-aware".

I fixed it **in the extracted copy only**, and pinned it with a test that formats under two languages and asserts the results differ. That's the only way to catch this class of bug: both spellings look identical in review and both produce a plausible date. The divergence from the platform copy is recorded in the file's header so the two don't drift silently.

**I have not touched the platform's 31 sites.** That's a sweep across code outside this slice, and whether to take it now is your call. It's mechanical — the same `undefined` → `currentLocale()` substitution — but it touches Home widgets, the public booking page and the aggregate layer, so it wants its own verification rather than being folded into an extraction.

Platform web tests still 435 green, OSS suites 1,383 green. All four repos staged.

content.text:
S5's component pass is done. `@cordango/web-controls` now has the model layer plus 21 components, 235 tests, both bundle formats building at 128 kB.

**The interesting finding is that `commands.js` split much better than the plan assumed.** The plan said it stays out because "the REST shape belongs to the app" — half right. Thirteen of its nineteen exports are pure manifest reads: which transitions a record may take from the state it's in, whether a guard currently allows a command, how commands index by placement. Only six touch transport. What a command *means* is identical in a generated app and on the platform; only how one is sent differs. It was sitting next to `axios` by accident of file layout.

So the pure half moved and the transport stayed, and that's what let the process stepper travel with **no seam at all** rather than needing a command-invoker injected as planned.

Also moved: 20 of 27 `Ui*` components turned out to be entirely host-free, plus `theme.js` (328 lines, imports only `vue`, and `optionAccent` needed it).

**Two packaging defects, both caught by consuming the built bundle rather than trusting it:**

`chart.js` was being bundled despite being a declared dependency. That's 537 kB down to **128 kB** once externalised, and more importantly a consumer no longer gets a second copy pinned to whatever version we happened to build against.

The `"./styles"` export pointed at `dist/style.css` while Vite was writing `dist/web-controls.css`. Every consumer doing `import '@cordango/web-controls/styles'` would have failed. Vite's default CSS name derives from the library name, so a rename would have silently broken it again — it's now pinned explicitly with that noted.

**Still not moved:** the data table (1,231 lines), field renderer, kanban board and reference pickers. Each reaches into its host for data — `data.js`, `me.js`, the toast bus — and those seams are the next pass. The field renderer is blocked behind the reference picker specifically, since it composes one.

Platform web still 435 green, package 235 green, all four repos staged.

content.text:
S5 is complete. All 31 components are in the package — the data-bound half moved once the seam was cut. 237 tests, 251 kB.

**The seam came out smaller than the plan sketched: five functions, not an interface.** Most of what looked like host dependency wasn't. `me.js` was already built on an injected user id, so it moved whole. `refState.js` is 33 pure lines. `isPersonField` turned out to read three properties of a field — it was filed under the data layer because that's where the person directory gets fetched, which made a predicate look like a network concern.

What genuinely differs between the platform and a generated app is: where records come from, where a file lives, what a link points at, where table preferences are kept, and how a message reaches the screen. `src/host.js` holds exactly those, and **every default is inert rather than clever** — an unwired directory answers empty so a chip renders an id, an unwired route answers null so a link renders as text. A host can adopt one seam at a time and watch behaviour appear, instead of having to satisfy the whole interface before the first component renders.

**Four packaging defects, all found by consuming the built bundle rather than trusting it.** Two I mentioned last time (`chart.js` bundled, CSS export path wrong). Two new ones:

`vue-i18n` was marked optional in `peerDependenciesMeta` while three components call `useI18n()` directly. A consumer trusting that would install the package and hit a resolve error on first render.

The interesting one: **`mediaUrl` was exported by both `theme.js` and `host.js`** — theme's builds a brand-asset URL from an explicit API base, host's is the attachment seam. Two `export *` sources offering one name is ambiguous, and ES modules resolve that by **dropping it silently**. The package shipped without `mediaUrl` at all. The build reported success; the only symptom would have been a consumer getting `undefined is not a function`. # @cordango/web-controls

Generic Vue 3 and Vuetify controls shared by Cordango Platform and by the standalone applications the
Cordango generator produces.

> Status: pre-alpha. Nothing here is published to npm yet and the surface changes without notice.

## What is in it today

**The model layer.** Manifest reading and field formatting, the command model (which transitions a
record may take, whether a guard allows a command), theming, filter memory, responsive breakpoints,
the date-surface windowing behind timelines and calendars, and the table composables: filtering,
grouping, tree rows, subtree aggregates, semantic dates.

**Thirty-one components.** The presentational primitives (buttons, chips, links, avatars, sheets,
tables, text and select inputs, meters, peeks, timezone and slug fields), the chart, the process
stepper, and the data-bound half: the data table, field renderer, kanban board, reference and person
pickers, facet select, weekly hours and cell editor.

237 tests.

## What belongs here

Low-level building blocks that any business application needs and that carry no product opinion:

data table, form inputs, field renderer, reference picker, person picker, organization picker, board,
calendar, timeline, chart, process stepper, command button, money and date inputs, filter controls,
layout primitives.

## What does not belong here

Anything that only makes sense inside the commercial platform: audit center, AI assistant,
marketplace administration, governance, cross-app explorer, platform administration, platform search.
Those live in the product, not in a generic controls package.

Also deliberately absent: the REST client, the router, and any global store. A control never decides
where data comes from. Everything a control needs from its host arrives through the plugin options
or through props, which is what lets the same component serve a multi-tenant platform and a
single-tenant generated app without knowing which one it is in.

That line moved once during the extraction and it is worth knowing why. `commands.js` looked like
host code because it sat next to `axios`, but thirteen of its nineteen exports only read a manifest
and a record: which transitions are available from the state a record is in, whether a guard allows
a command. What a command MEANS is identical everywhere; only how one is sent differs. So the
meaning is in this package and the sending is not.

## Using it

```js
import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { CordangoControls } from '@cordango/web-controls'
import '@cordango/web-controls/styles'

createApp(App).use(CordangoControls, {
  locale: () => i18n.global.locale.value,   // which language to format in

  // The five things a control cannot work out for itself. Every one is optional and falls back to
  // something inert, so you can wire one at a time and watch behaviour appear.
  people: () => api.get('/platform/person'),      // the person directory
  media: (ref) => `${API}${ref}`,                 // where a stored file lives
  route: (target, id) => `/app/${target.entity}/${id}`,  // where a referenced record opens
  loadTableSettings: (handle, table) => api.get(...),    // one person's column preferences
  saveTableSettings: (handle, table, s) => api.put(...),
  toast: (message, color) => snackbar.show(message, color),
})
```

Vue, Vuetify and vue-i18n are peer dependencies. The host owns those versions.

## Development

```
npm install
npm run build
npm test
```

Tests are plain `node --test` over the pure modules. Components are verified by the applications that
consume them rather than by a headless DOM here.

## License

Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Time off

Somebody requests time off. Their manager approves or declines it. A calendar shows who is away.

One entity, three roles, three screens. Read it after `expenses` to see how differently the same
shape can be presented.

## What to look at

**`views/screens/schedule.cordango.yaml`** is the interesting file, and the reason to read this one.
It is a calendar, and a calendar needs to know which month it is showing:

```yaml
screen: schedule
label: Who's off
state:
  - key: cursor
    type: date
    default: '{{today}}'
```

That `state` block is screen state. The cursor belongs to the page rather than to any record, it
starts at today, and moving it is what pages the calendar back and forth. It is the mechanism behind
every screen that has a position of its own, and this is the smallest example of it.

**`workflows/lifecycles/approval.cordango.yaml`** is deliberately shorter than the expenses one.
Approval is a decision with two outcomes, and modelling it with six states would describe the
software rather than the business.

**`roles/`** shows the same three-way split as `expenses` over completely different subject matter,
which is worth comparing: an employee sees their own requests, a manager sees the queue, an admin
sees everything.

## Running it

```
cordango check
cordango check --target standalone
```

## Structure

```
cordango.yaml              the workspace: which applications are installed
apps/time-off/
  app.cordango.yaml        the application's name, and the order things appear in
  entities/                what it stores
  workflows/               lifecycles and automations
  roles/                   who may do what
  views/                   collections, screens, and one record's detail
```
