Definition. To add behaviour, add files of your own beside them — a hook registered in its own file,
a controller with its own route, a page the router picks up. That is the intended way to extend a
generated application, and it survives every rebuild.

## Changing the schema

After generation this is a normal EF Core project:

```
cd api
dotnet ef migrations add WhateverYouChanged
```

The application applies pending migrations at startup.

## Who may do what

Permissions come from the definition's roles and are compiled into `AppPermissions.cs`: which
entities a role may read, create, change and delete, which fields it may see or set, and which
commands it may run. The rules are enforced on every route, and a field a role cannot read never
appears in a response — not in the record, and not in a message rendered from it.

  controller — including on a controller you add later without reading this.

  the API should go through it.

  enumerated. Any signed-in caller who *has* a reference can fetch the file behind it, including one
  attached to a record their role cannot read.

  the message is translated. Exception detail is logged, never sent.

`api/Cordango/` and `web/vendor/cordango-web-controls/` are the Cordango runtime, licensed under
Apache-2.0 and carrying their own headers. You may keep them, change them, or replace them.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <RootNamespace>Cordango</RootNamespace>

    RULE 0 — this project is the portable core, and this ItemGroup is the whole claim.

    ZERO ProjectReferences and exactly ONE package. Everything an application definition means lives
    here and can be reasoned about without a database, a container, a web host or a model provider:

      Definition/   the contract. Schema gate, semantic validation, normalizer, computed-expression
                    language, core-app registry, definition hash.
      Cord/         the semantic model authored source is written in, and the lowering to a
                    definition. A function of the model ALONE.
      Compile/      definition to runtime manifest, plus the one validation pipeline every caller
                    goes through.
      Semantics/    condition and template evaluation, shared by every host that runs an app.
      Tokens/       the access-token format. One credential is written by a Cordango server and read
                    by the CLI, on opposite sides of a boundary this repository enforces, so it can
                    live in neither of them. A second implementation was the alternative, and a
                    security-relevant encoding with two implementations drifts at the checksum first
                    and at the hash second, where neither drift shows up as an error: it shows up as
                    tokens that verify on one side and not the other. It is BCL-only, so it carries
                    nothing into the portable boundary and does not earn an assembly of its own.

    MUST NOT be added here, ever: any web framework, EF or Npgsql, any AI or provider client, any
    tenant or hosting concern. Hosts adapt to this project; it never reaches back.

    Not a convention anyone has to remember: tests/Compiler.Tests/BoundaryTests.cs asserts the
    compiled assembly's reference set against an allowlist and this file's shape against the rule.
  -->

    <PackageReference Include="JsonSchema.Net" Version="9.2.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

<ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="..\Cordango.SourceGen\Cordango.SourceGen.csproj" />

  <!--
    THE SCAFFOLD, EMBEDDED — and note what is NOT here: a ProjectReference to Cordango.Standalone.

    A generated application's runtime is emitted as SOURCE, so what this project needs from
    Cordango.Standalone is its files, not its types. Referencing the project would compile fine and
    drag Microsoft.AspNetCore.App and EF Core into the CLI, which is a console application that
    never serves a request. So the files are embedded by path instead, the same way the compiler
    embeds the schemas it validates against.

    Two sets, and the distinction matters for licensing as well as for paths:

      Runtime/   Cordango.Standalone's own .cs files. OUR code, Apache-2.0, headers intact, landing
                 under api/Cordango/ in the generated project. Compiled and tested in this
                 repository, so the code an application runs is code with tests behind it.
      Template/  what an application looks like before any entity exists. The USER's code: no
                 Cordango headers, and the project file carries a .template suffix so that a stray
                 `dotnet build` in this repository never tries to compile a file full of {{...}}.

    RecursiveDir bakes in the host's path separator, so ScaffoldFiles normalises to '/' on read —
    without that, the same definition would generate different file paths on Windows and Linux and
    the determinism tests would be measuring the build machine.
  -->
  <ItemGroup>
    <EmbeddedResource Include="..\Cordango.Standalone\**\*.cs"
                      Exclude="..\Cordango.Standalone\Templates\**;..\Cordango.Standalone\bin\**;..\Cordango.Standalone\obj\**"
                      LogicalName="Runtime/%(RecursiveDir)%(Filename)%(Extension)" />
    <EmbeddedResource Include="..\Cordango.Standalone\Templates\**\*"
                      LogicalName="Template/%(RecursiveDir)%(Filename)%(Extension)" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <!-- Outside the project tree, so `dotnet watch` would not notice an edit, and an embedded
       resource cannot be hot-reloaded regardless. Watch items make a save rebuild instead of
       silently serving the previous scaffold. -->
  <ItemGroup>
    <Watch Include="..\Cordango.Standalone\**\*.cs" Exclude="..\Cordango.Standalone\bin\**;..\Cordango.Standalone\obj\**" />
    <Watch Include="..\Cordango.Standalone\Templates\**\*" />
  </ItemGroup>

# Permission decision fixtures

These files are the contract between two implementations of the same four rules.

Cordango Platform resolves an App Definition's `roles` into an effective access decision with its own
code. A standalone application generated by this toolchain resolves them with *different* code, in
`Cordango.Standalone.Security.PermissionResolver`. That duplication is deliberate: sharing the
implementation would mean a change made for one product's reasons silently altering the other's
enforcement, and enforcement is the last place to accept a surprise.

What duplication normally costs is drift, and drift in a permission rule does not announce itself —
it shows up as somebody seeing a field they should not, on one product only, months later. So the
rules are pinned here as **data**, and both implementations are asserted against the same data by
their own test suites. Two implementations that must agree, and a test that fails the moment they
stop.

## The four rules these files pin

1. **Roles union.** Any role the caller holds that allows an operation allows it.
2. **Specific beats wildcard, within one role.** A grant naming the entity replaces that role's `*`
   grant; it does not merge with it.
3. **Field rules resolve per role, then union.** A field's answer for one role is that role's
   explicit override if it has one, otherwise that role's entity-level default. Only then are the
   roles unioned. Unioning the defaults first and applying overrides afterwards gives a different —
   and wrong — answer.
4. **Commands are deny-by-default.** Update does not imply any command. Only a grant that names the
   command, or `*`, allows it.

## Format

```jsonc
{
  "name": "...",              // what this file is about
  "why": "...",               // the mistake it exists to catch
  "roles": [ ... ],           // exactly the definition's roles array
  "cases": [
    {
      "roleKeys": ["agent"],  // the roles the caller holds
      "entity": "ticket",
      "expect":   { "create": false, "read": true, "update": true, "delete": false },
      "fields":   { "salary": { "read": false, "update": false } },  // optional
      "commands": { "close": true, "purge": false }                  // optional
    }
  ]
}
```

`expect` is the entity-level answer. `fields` and `commands` are checked only where named, so a case
stays about the one thing it is testing.

## Adding a case

Add it here first, then run both suites. If they disagree with each other, one implementation has a
bug. If they agree with each other and disagree with the fixture, the fixture is wrong — or the rule
is not what you thought, which is worth finding out before shipping it.

The fixtures are hand-written rather than recorded from either implementation. Recording would make
one of them the definition of correct, and would enshrine its bugs as the contract the other has to
match.

The binary and the workspace format are now `cordango`. **Next = the standalone SOURCE GENERATOR** (`cordango build --target standalone` → a conventional ASP.NET Core + EF + Vue application you own), which is slices S4–S10 of the split plan. Everything below is the pre-split history of this track. **Phases 0+1 SHIPPED 2026-08-13**, and **`cordango` now CONNECTS to an instance (2026-08-13)** — built + tested (3,395 backend + 412 web green), NOT live-verified. This was §13 phase 6 work moved to the front on purpose: the disconnect a user actually hits is building an app with an agent in a Git checkout and having no way to see it running, and the hosted (or local Docker) instance already IS a runtime, so connecting to it solves localhost and hosted with one implementation and does not spend the PostgreSQL spike. New: `cordango login / whoami / publish / logout`, all `--json`, the only commands in the CLI that touch a network. **Credential** = `AppBuilder.AccessTokens`, a BCL-only project both the API and the CLI reference, because a format written by one and parsed by the other must not have two implementations; two spellings, one secret — a **Personal Access Token** (needs `--instance`) and a **Cordango Access Exchange Token** (carries the instance origin + tenant, so `cordango login <token>` is the whole command). The address inside an exchange token is a **claim, never an authority**: login asks the server which tenant the key really belongs to and refuses on disagreement. Minted under the avatar menu → **Personal Access Keys** (`/account/keys`), shown once, only the SHA-256 stored, `access_keys` table + migration. **Authentication** = a policy scheme forwards on the `Authorization` header's shape to either OpenIddict validation or the access-key handler, and a key acts AS ITS OWNER, so a CLI reaches exactly the endpoints a person does under exactly the same policies — there is no CLI-specific API to drift. **Publish** = `POST /api/apps/publish`, import's non-admin sibling: open to any member because every lookup and write is owner-scoped, and it REFUSES a taken handle rather than suffixing it (a suffixed handle is what would make the next publish from the same checkout create a second app). A changed definition at an unchanged version is refused (`--force` overrides) so `app_versions` never claims one version was two documents; an identical republish is a no-op, compared by `DefinitionHash` because jsonb reorders keys. Credentials live outside the repo (`CORD_CONFIG_DIR` overridable) keyed by the committed `workspaceId`. **Still open: `cord pull`, seeding on publish, and reconciling an app deleted from the workspace with one still live.** **Next = phase 2, the packaged cross-platform PostgreSQL spike** (Windows x64 / macOS arm64 / Linux x64: `initdb`, clean shutdown, crash recovery, non-ASCII paths, notarization of the bundled binaries, glibc + libicu baseline). The plan calls this the highest-risk slice and says to prove it before any packaging or MCP work. Storage is decided: **Postgres packaged inside the single install**, no SQLite, no second engine. The spike's runtime also inherits a design requirement from the 2026-08-20 security batch: **first-run admin setup** — `cordango run` prompts for admin credentials on the very first run (or a one-time browser setup screen on first open); the server no longer seeds a default admin outside Development. **Deliberately not built:** `cordango run`, watch mode, `cord mcp`, `cord test` | — |

content.content:
user-grant/team-grant/no-grant × CRUD × wildcard, fieldOverrides read-strip + write-reject, audit =
  real user, personal-app grants inert, `/ai/records` gate, cross-tenant + unknown-role grant rejection,
  the filter/sort oracle regression). **Full solution 161 green** (Definition 45, Runtime 75, Api 41).

**Also shipped (2026-07-12): LIVE generation streaming in the Studio.** The provider streams SSE
from Melious/Anthropic (`stream: true`) when a callback is attached: thinking deltas + the tool-call
JSON as it's written, reassembled into the exact non-streaming response shape (tool-use extraction
unchanged). `IGenerationProvider.GenerateAsync` gained optional `onDelta`; generate/refine forward
it over the existing SignalR hub as throttled (150ms) `stream` events — thinking TEXT is forwarded,
the JSON phase sends ~token counters only. Streaming requests drop the 120s HttpClient cap (long
generations used to DIE at it); liveness = a 90s per-event inactivity guard (abort + retry, never
hang). Studio Stage-3 now shows: live "Thinking" tail, "Writing the app definition" + token counter,
a stall warning after 60s of silence, 10-min axios timeout + friendly timeout/connection-lost
errors (an api restart mid-run previously left an eternal spinner — the 2026-07-12 "stuck 10 min"
root cause). NOTE: glm-5.2 emits thinking blocks now (handled; ~45s typical generation). Live
in-browser pass of the streaming view OWED (docker was down at verification time; builds green,
161/161 tests).

**Remaining milestone:** **M4** connections store (encrypted secrets via DataProtection-in-DB,
slack/n8n/smtp/http test-connection, connectionRef build gate, SMTP resolution dogfoods the store). 

## Latest (2026-08-20 — WEB CONTROLS: the pure layer extracted, and a live localisation bug found ✅)

`@cordango/web-controls` has real content: the model layer, twenty-one components, 235 tests, and
both bundle formats building at 128 kB. Modules: `manifest.js`, `commands.js`, `theme.js`,
`filterMemory.js`, `responsive.js`, `formatting.js`, the six date-surface modules behind timelines
and calendars, and the five table composables. Components: the presentational primitives, the chart,
and the process stepper.

**`commands.js` split better than the plan assumed.** The plan said it stays out because "the REST
shape belongs to the app", and half of that is right. But thirteen of its nineteen exports are pure
manifest reads — which transitions a record may take from the state it is in, whether a guard allows
a command — and only six touch transport. What a command MEANS is identical in a generated
application and on the platform; only how one is sent differs. So the pure half moved and the
transport stayed, which is what let the process stepper travel with no seam at all.

**The data-bound half moved too**, once the seam was cut: data table, field renderer, kanban board,
reference and person pickers, facet select, weekly hours, cell editor. 31 components, 237 tests,
251 kB.

**The seam came out at five functions, not the interface the plan sketched.** `me.js` was already
built on an injected user id, so it moved whole; `refState.js` is 33 pure lines; `isPersonField`
turned out to read three properties of a field and belonged with the manifest rather than with the
data layer it was filed under. What genuinely differs between the hosted platform and a generated
application is: where records come from, where a file lives, what a link points at, where table
preferences are kept, and how a message reaches the screen. `src/host.js` holds exactly those, every
default inert rather than clever — an unwired directory answers empty so a chip renders an id, an
unwired route answers null so a link renders as text. A host adopts one at a time and watches
behaviour appear instead of having to satisfy the whole interface before the first render.

**Twenty of twenty-seven `Ui*` components turned out to be host-free**, and every import in the
moved set is internal or a peer dependency. Only `formatting.js` reached into the host, for
`currentLocale()`. That is now
`src/locale.js`, a settable source defaulting to English, wired by the `CordangoControls` plugin.
Deliberately NOT falling back to `navigator.language`: a control that guessed would pass every test
on an English machine and render German dates on the reviewer's laptop.

**A LIVE PLATFORM DEFECT came out of smoke-testing the package.** Formatting the same date under
`en` and `de` produced identical output, because `manifest.js` formats with
`toLocaleString(undefined, …)` — and `undefined` is the BROWSER's locale, not the application's. A
German workspace therefore renders English dates for anyone whose browser is English, and the
reverse. This is exactly the rule the 2026-08-08 localisation work established (`toLocale*` is
forbidden, everything goes through `i18n/formatting.js`), and ~30 call sites were converted then.
**31 were missed and are still live in `web/src`**: 7 in `manifest.js`, 6 in `home/widgets.js`, 2 in
`home/HomeWidgetCard.vue`, 2 in `public/BookingPage.vue`, 1 in `blockAggregate.js`, and the rest
across the views. `manifest.js` even carries a comment calling its formatters "locale-aware".

**Four packaging defects, every one caught by consuming the built bundle rather than trusting it.**
`chart.js` was being bundled despite being a declared dependency (537 kB down to 128 kB once
external, and a consumer no longer gets a second copy pinned to whatever we built against). The
`"./styles"` export pointed at `dist/style.css` while Vite wrote `dist/web-controls.css`, so
importing the stylesheet would have failed for everyone. `vue-i18n` was marked optional in
`peerDependenciesMeta` while three components call `useI18n()` directly, which is a promise the code
does not keep. And `mediaUrl` was exported by BOTH `theme.js` (a brand asset from an explicit base)
and `host.js` (the attachment seam) — **two `export *` sources offering one name is ambiguous, and
ES modules resolve that by dropping it silently**, so the package shipped without `mediaUrl` and
nothing said so. The build reported success; the only symptom would have been a consumer getting
`undefined is not a function`. Now disambiguated (the seam keeps the plain name, theme's is
`brandAssetUrl`) and pinned by `surface.test.js`, which fails on any ambiguous star export and on
any module the index does not reach.

The extracted copy is fixed and pinned by a test that formats under two languages and asserts the
results differ, which is the only way to catch this: both spellings look the same and both produce a
plausible date. **The platform copy is NOT fixed** — that is 31 sites across code I did not come
here to change, and it is Tim's call whether to take it now. The divergence is recorded in the
extracted file's header so the two do not silently drift.

## Latest (2026-08-20 — `cordango import`, and the examples repository is no longer empty ✅)

Tim asked where the examples went. Nothing was lost: the old samples all moved into
`oss/cordango/tests/corpus/` (13 reference apps, crm, budget-planner, the 200-file CordSource
specimen) and `tests/fixtures/` (historical, interactive, invalid, raw-allowlist). Those stay put
because `dotnet test Cordango.slnx` is pinned to them and has to pass from a standalone clone. What
was genuinely missing is the examples repository, whose README I had written in S0 listing four
examples that did not exist.

shape belongs to the app", and half of that is right. But thirteen of its nineteen exports are pure

S6 of the split plan. `Cordango.Standalone` is the runtime a generated application runs on, and
`Templates/` is what that application looks like before a single entity exists: host, sign-in,
directory, media, health, Docker packaging, Vue shell, en+de. **The scaffold materialises and
`dotnet build` passes** — asserted by a test that writes it to a temp directory and runs the real
SDK over it, because nothing else in the repository compiles those files. 33 new tests; OSS suite
1,446 green from a clone with no platform above it.

**The APIGenerator assessment came out "pattern, throughout"** —
[oss/cordango/docs/apigenerator-assessment.md](oss/cordango/docs/apigenerator-assessment.md).
Tim's architecture survives intact (generic machinery once, thin regenerable per-entity types,
`IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` as the mapping seam, lifecycle hooks as the extension point, EF
migrations as the schema story). Four things change, and each is the difference between a runtime
framework and a code generator:

- **Registration is generated, not discovered.** `TCDev.APIGenerator` scans assemblies for `[Api]`,
  closes a generic controller over each type it finds, and rewrites routes from an attribute. That
  machinery answers at startup a question we answer at build time, and it costs determinism (scan
  order), legibility (a controller you cannot grep for), and a failure mode (missing route at
  runtime instead of a compile error). So: one six-line derived class per entity, emitted.
- **Hooks live in the container, not on the entity.** The prior art puts hook methods on the POCO,
  which is fine for hand-written code and a trap for generated code: the entity file is precisely
  the file the generator overwrites, so the one place the design invites your logic is the one place
  it cannot survive.
- **Tracking fields are stamped in one typed place.** See below.
- **Migrations are files the user owns** (`MigrationsScaffolder`, pinned id, `Database.Migrate()`),
  not `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` diffing the model at every startup.

**Seven defects found in the prior art, recorded because a generator amplifies.** The sharpest is an
`IsAssignableFrom`/`IsAssignableTo` inversion at six sites: the operands are the wrong way round, so
the condition is false for every entity. Nothing throws. **Tracking fields are simply never
populated**, an entity opting into `ISoftDelete` is **hard-deleted instead**, and in a multi-tenant
deployment the tenant query filter never applies. Also: `async void` on create and update (so the
controller's save races the before-create hook, and a hook that refuses a write refuses it after the
write), `oldRecord = newRecord` assigning a parameter, an after-create branch that calls
`BeforeCreate` again, an unconditional deref of `cacheOptions`, `e.Id.ToString() == id.ToString()`,
`ex.Message` on the wire from two places, and a Postgres provider whose `OnConfiguring` calls
`UseSqlServer` through an extension method that is `private`. The lesson taken: a hand-written
type-relationship check with no test on the negative case is worth **eliminating** rather than
getting right — `ChangeTracker.Entries<IHasTrackingFields>()` cannot be written backwards and still
compile.

**Permissions: two implementations, one contract.** The generated application resolves the
definition's roles with its own code, deliberately not sharing the platform's — sharing would mean a
change made for standalone's reasons altering platform enforcement. Drift is **detected** instead:
`oss/cordango/tests/fixtures/permissions/*.json` holds hand-written decisions (roles union, specific
beats wildcard, field rules per role before unioning, commands deny-by-default), and **both suites
assert the same files** — `PermissionFixtureTests` in `Standalone.Tests` and a twin in
`Runtime.Tests`. Hand-written rather than recorded from either side, because recording makes one
side's bugs the definition of correct. Both agree today. Also removed: `AppBuilder.Runtime.csproj`
still carried a `ProjectReference` to the reverted `Cordango.Authorization`, which built with a
warning nobody read.

**A security hole closed while writing it.** `PermissionResolver` falls back to read-only when a
definition declares no roles, which is reasonable for a colleague and terrible for the internet:
without an authentication check first, deploying such an application publishes every row to
anonymous callers, and nothing in the definition hints that it would. Nobody signed in now gets
nothing, checked **before** the no-roles default. Antiforgery is global
(`AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` as a filter, so a controller added later inherits it) and
pinned by a test that reads the filter collection rather than the source.

**Two defects the new tests caught in my own work.** `Resources/messages.de.json` and
`messages.en.json` were **silently compiled into `de/` and `en/` satellite assemblies** instead of
into the generator, because the SDK reads a dotted segment in an embedded resource name as a
culture. Clean build, no warning, and every generated application would have shipped with no
translated messages — fixed with `WithCulture="false"`, and the argument for asserting the emitted
file list rather than trusting the glob. And `Program.cs` registered `AppDbContext` twice, once as
itself and once as `CordangoDbContext`, which would have given every request two change trackers and
two connections — so a hook's pending changes would have been invisible to the save meant to include
them.

**Not done, and said out loud:** the web half of the acceptance check. `web/package.json` depends on
`@cordango/web-controls` at `file:./vendor/cordango-web-controls`, and nothing vendors that bundle
yet — the controls package builds to a `dist/` that is not committed, so embedding it would break a
clean clone rather than fix anything. Vendoring lands with the Vue emitters at S9, and `npm ci &&
npm run build` lands with it. The scaffold's Dockerfile already handles the lock-file question
honestly (`npm ci` when one exists, `npm install` when it does not, because a lock file records a
resolution against the registry and the generator does not go to the network).

**The generator still refuses.** `dotnet-vue` has a working scaffold and no entity emitters, so
`Generate` answers CORD2300 rather than writing an application that starts, serves a login page, and
contains not one row of the business its definition describes. **Next = S7**, the backend emitters:
POCOs, `IEntityTypeConfiguration`, hooks, `AppPermissions`, `CommandService`, and the EF-scaffolded
migration with a pinned id.

"""
s = s.replace(anchor, new + anchor, 1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8',newline='').write(s)
print('ok')
PY

content.content:
# Cordango

Cordango is an open application language and deterministic compiler for building complete business
applications. Define what your application should do, generate conventional source code, own it, and
deploy it anywhere.

There is no runtime dependency on Cordango in what you generate. No license server, no account, no
model API. The generated project is an ordinary ASP.NET Core and Vue application that keeps working
whether or not this project does.

> Status: pre-alpha. The standalone generator is under construction and nothing here is stable yet.

## What is in this repository

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `src/Cordango.Compiler` | The App Definition contract: schema gate, semantic validation, normalizer, the Cord semantic model, and the compiler that turns a definition into a runtime manifest. |
| `src/Cordango.Authorization` | Permission semantics: role grants, entity access, field-level read and write rules. One implementation, shared by every host. |
| `src/Cordango.AccessTokens` | The access token format used when the CLI talks to a Cordango instance. |
| `src/Cordango.Cli` | The `cordango` command. |
| `src/Cordango.SourceGen` | The generator SDK: capabilities, target validation, the file runner, the external generator protocol. |
| `src/Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue` | The first-party generator. ASP.NET Core, EF Core, PostgreSQL, Vue 3, Vuetify. |
| `src/Cordango.Standalone` | The scaffold every generated application is built on: authentication, authorization, Organizations, People, infrastructure. |
| `schemas/` | The App Definition JSON Schema and its composed sources. |
| `samples/` | Application definitions used as the conformance corpus. |
| `tests/` | Compiler, generator, determinism and compatibility suites. |

## The two products

Cordango Open Source builds **one application**. It has its own backend, frontend, database, users,
authentication, permissions, Organizations and People. It is not multi-tenant, it contains no AI at
runtime, and it belongs to whoever generated it.

Cordango Platform connects, operates and governs **many applications** as one company system: shared
people and organizations across apps, cross-app references, audit and record history, governance, AI,
search, marketplace and managed hosting. That is a separate, commercial product.

The same application definition works in both places. What differs is what each target supports, and
every target says so out loud rather than silently dropping what it cannot do.

content.content:
---
name: cord-oss-cli
description: "The OSS `cordango` CLI track — the REPOSITORY SPLIT shipped 2026-08-20 (compiler + CLI now live in the public cordango repo, mounted as a submodule); storage settled as packaged Postgres (never SQLite); the scary Postgres coupling is multi-host coupling a one-process local runtime drops"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 03b8c430-f5d4-4e35-b3a2-974ae80f5759
  modified: 2026-08-20T19:09:39.734Z
---

**THE CODE LEFT THIS REPOSITORY on 2026-08-20.** `oss/cordango` is a git SUBMODULE of
github.com/cordango/cordango (siblings: `oss/web-controls`, `oss/examples`), holding
`Cordango.Compiler` (the old Definition + Cord + the pure compile layer + the credential format)
and `Cordango.Cli`, plus the schema and the conformance corpus under `tests/corpus/`. The claim is
a COMMAND, not a diagram: `dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` passes from a clone with no
platform above it. `AppBuilder.Oss.slnx` and `AppBuilder.Cord.slnx` are deleted — they existed to
make extraction checkable while the code was still here.

**Six things about the split that will not be obvious from the tree:**

- **A cross-repo move is never `git mv`.** Filesystem copy, `git add` in the submodule, `git rm` in
  the parent, two independent commits, then the parent's pointer bump. Fighting Git over this costs
  an hour.
- **STANDALONE SECURITY IS DELIBERATELY SEPARATE — settled, and do not reopen it.** Tim's rule:
  a generated app uses stock ASP.NET Core Identity and shares NOTHING of the platform's
  authentication, because coupling the two makes the platform less secure. **I conflated two things
  and was wrong about one of them.** Authentication (who the caller is) was never shareable and is
  not interesting. Authorization (what the definition's `roles[]` MEAN — union across roles,
  specific beats `*`, field override else role default, commands deny-by-default) is not security
  infrastructure at all; it is definition interpretation, the same family as computed expressions.
  I extracted it into a `Cordango.Authorization` project on that reasoning and Tim reverted it,
  correctly — the objection that survives is **blast radius, not secrecy**: a shared assembly means
  a change made for standalone reasons can alter platform enforcement.
  **The resolution is to DETECT drift, not prevent it**: the scaffold gets its own permission code,
  and a `(definition, roles, entity, field, operation) → expected decision` fixture generated from
  the platform evaluator lives in the public repo as DATA and is asserted by both suites.
  `PermissionEvaluator` + `FieldProjection` stay in `AppBuilder.Runtime`, unpublished.
- **No one-file assemblies.** `Cordango.AccessTokens` was a project holding a single BCL-only file
  and read as odd; it is now `Cordango.Compiler/Tokens/`. It still cannot live in the CLI alone — a
  server writes the credential and the CLI reads it, so two implementations would drift at the
  checksum first and the hash second, neither of which surfaces as an error.
- **`tests/corpus/`, not `samples/`.** There is a whole `cordango/examples` repository; a second
  directory called samples inside the compiler was two things claiming one name. What lives there is
  the conformance corpus the suites are pinned to.
- **Every source file carries an SPDX licence header**, enforced by `LicenceHeaderTests` rather than
  a sweep that rots. The exemption is the interesting part: the Budget Planner specimen's `.cord.ts`
  files are EXAMPLE APPLICATION SOURCE, and stamping our copyright on the thing a reader is meant to
  copy says the wrong thing. **Generated output gets no Cordango header either** — it belongs to the
  user.
- **Anything anchored on the repo root is now ambiguous.** `Corpus.RepoRoot()` resolves the
  *Cordango* root, so two platform tests silently started writing their review artifacts INTO the
  public checkout. If a test writes a file, check which repository it lands in.

The binary and the workspace format are `cordango` / `cordango.yaml` / `*.cordango.yaml` /
`.cordango/`. Old names are still read and `fmt` migrates them — and `fmt` had to learn that a
filename change IS drift, because the content is byte-identical and a content-comparing formatter
called a legacy workspace canonical and walked away. Token prefixes `cord_pat`/`cord_cxt` did NOT
rename (wire format, shared with the server and with secret scanners). Credentials moved to the
`cordango` application-data directory with a read-only fallback to the old one.

**The CLI no longer ships a database driver.** It had referenced `AppBuilder.Runtime` for
`CandidateValidator` alone and inherited Npgsql for it. Moving the validator rather than copying it
was the fix the old csproj comment had already predicted.

Phases 0+1 (2026-08-13) remain: `new / add app / check / build / inspect / apply / fmt / doctor /
version`, all `--json`, offline and token-free. Still no database, no `cordango run`, no
`cordango mcp`, no watch mode.

**S4 SHIPPED 2026-08-20 — the capability gate exists before any generator does.**
`cordango check --target standalone` / `cordango targets` answer from DECLARED capability data, so a
target is publishable as a claim before its emitters exist. Three things worth remembering:
**(a) capabilities carry REASONS, not booleans** — every schema value is supported or withheld with
a sentence, enforced by a test, same doctrine as `CordWordMap.Withheld`; **(b) blocks are NOT only
under `pages`/`views`** — an entity's own `detail` carries them, which is where ventures hides its
audit block, and the first walker missed it; **(c) SCOPE IS SET FROM THE LANGUAGE, NOT FROM THE
EMITTERS.** I first declared the target from what would be easy to build and measured the result;
Tim rejected it. **"One application" is a statement about how many, not about how elaborate one may
be** — a standalone target that cannot build the Budget Planner is not selling the calculation
plane. So every screen and the whole calculation plane are IN (gantt, timeline, orgchart, intake,
answers, embeds, widgets, series, `prev()`, windowed/matched rollups). OUT is only what needs OTHER
applications or a model: cross-app references, `relatedApps`, `enrich`, and record history
(architecture doc §21, platform-only). **EVERY refusal is written as an UPSELL, and a test enforces
the shape**: name the feature as a Cordango Platform capability, say what the platform does with it,
say what a standalone build carries instead, and give both ways forward (change the app, or change
where it runs). I first argued relatedApps was different in kind because with one application the
question is unanswerable rather than unimplemented; Tim rejected that and he is right — from the
reader's side both are "the platform does this and this build does not", and cross-application data
is exactly what the platform sells. A refusal reading as "unsupported" turns a sales conversation
into a bug report. This makes S8 (the recompute cascade) materially bigger; Tim's call is to hit it in plan
order, and it must come out as GENERIC DETERMINISTIC generated code, not a hand-tuned engine.

**NEXT = the rest of the standalone SOURCE GENERATOR**, now the headline OSS deliverable and a DIFFERENT track
from `cordango run`: `cordango build --target standalone` emits a conventional ASP.NET Core + EF Core
+ Vue application the user owns, with no AI, no audit, no multi-tenancy and no cross-app anything.
Plan: `~/.claude/plans/heres-a-pretty-extensive-glimmering-lobster.md` (slices S4–S10). Both run
tracks live — `cordango run` simulates the PLATFORM locally for platform users; the generator serves
people who want one app and no platform at all. The generated backend follows Tim's own
TCDev.APIGenerator pattern (generic controller + `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly` DbContext +
lifecycle hooks in the scaffold, thin per-entity POCOs generated), with EF-native migrations.

**The runtime requirement is ONE INSTALL, not a particular engine.** Tim's words: "I do not want the
user to run 2 setups — if we can package a postgres WITH the app setup and it's just one setup via
CLI installable, that's fine." So SQLite was considered and is **not** wanted, and CordyOSS §7.2's
managed-Postgres recommendation already matches the intent. Never propose a second storage backend.

**Why that is cheaper than §7.2 implies** (measured 2026-08-13, not in the repo): app records are
already behind `IEntityStore` with a Postgres and an in-memory implementation. The genuinely
Postgres-shaped pieces — `pg_advisory` locks, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` as the turn-stream broker,
`tenant_{id}` schema-per-tenant — exist to coordinate **separate api/worker/ops hosts**. A
single-process local runtime drops them rather than porting them. The real remaining cost is the
control plane: EF Core + Npgsql, ~30 migrations, 26 `jsonb` column declarations.

**THE FILE FORMAT IS DECLARATIVE YAML, NOT OPERATIONS** (corrected and SHIPPED 2026-08-13). An
operation is a command log; source is a declaration. Ops exist because whole-DOCUMENT rewriting caused
destructive omissions on a 208KB AppDefinition — that lesson does not transfer to a 200-line
per-aggregate file, and a dropped field is caught by `git diff` locally and the diff screen in the
product. The ops layer is ~2,700 lines that may now largely die.

**`CordSource` is the format and it is TOTAL.** The forcing measurement: `CordDocument.Write` had
unwritable pointers for ALL 15 reference apps — an op cannot express a raw fragment and the whole
visual layer is one — so nothing could be written to files, and `CoCreationStore`'s
`if (!materialized.Complete) return []` means **every imported hosted app has zero `.cord` file rows
right now**. CordSource splits the LOWERED document, so it is total by construction and exactly
invertible (`Join(Split(d)) == d` by definition hash, asserted for all 15). A declaration may carry raw
where an operation may not — that rule is about what a MODEL emits, and a file writer is not in any

  `(roles, roleKeys, entity, field/command) \u2192 expected decision` cases that BOTH suites assert

  **HAND-WRITTEN, not recorded from the platform evaluator** \u2014 recording makes one side's bugs the
  definition of correct; hand-writing means both failing tells you the fixture is wrong and one
  failing tells you an implementation is. `PermissionEvaluator` + `FieldProjection` stay in
  `AppBuilder.Runtime`, unpublished (and a dangling `Cordango.Authorization` ProjectReference
  survived the revert as a build WARNING nobody read \u2014 now gone)."""

  in the OSS repo, embedded verbatim by `Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue` and written to
  `api/Cordango/` in the generated app. A test asserts the on-disk set equals the embedded set, so a
  file added and not embedded fails loudly. DotNetVue deliberately does NOT ProjectReference
  Standalone \u2014 that would drag ASP.NET Core + EF into the CLI, a console app that never serves a
  request.
- **The APIGenerator verdict is "pattern, throughout"** (`oss/cordango/docs/apigenerator-assessment.md`).
  Tim's architecture survives; four things change. **Registration is GENERATED, not discovered** \u2014
  reflection answers at startup a question we answer at build time and costs determinism, greppability
  and a compile-time failure mode. **Hooks live in the CONTAINER, not on the entity** \u2014 the entity

io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8',newline='').write(s)
print('ok')

content.text:
S6 is done. The scaffold exists, and it compiles.

**The APIGenerator assessment came out "pattern, throughout"** — nothing adopted as a dependency, nothing lifted verbatim. Your architecture survives intact: generic machinery once, thin regenerable per-entity types, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` as the mapping seam, hooks as the extension point, EF migrations as the schema story. Four things change, and each is the same difference — **a runtime framework meets its entities at startup; a generator meets them at build time**:

- **Registration is generated, not discovered.** The `[Api]` scan, the feature provider closing the generic controller, the route convention — all machinery answering at startup a question we answer at build time. It costs determinism (scan order), a controller you can't grep for, and a missing route at runtime instead of a compile error. So: one six-line derived class per entity.
- **Hooks live in the container.** The prior art puts them on the POCO, which is fine for hand-written code and a trap for generated code: the entity file is precisely the file the generator overwrites, so the one place the design invites your logic is the one place it can't survive.
- Tracking fields stamped once, where `ChangeTracker.Entries<IHasTrackingFields>()` can't be written backwards.
- Migrations as EF-scaffolded files you own, not `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` diffing at every startup.

**Seven defects found, recorded because a generator amplifies.** The headline: `typeof(T).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(IHasTrackingFields))` at six sites — operands reversed, so the condition is false for every entity. Nothing throws. **Tracking fields are never populated, `ISoftDelete` entities are hard-deleted instead, and the tenant query filter never applies.** Also `async void` on create and update, so the controller's save races the before-create hook and a hook that refuses a write refuses it *after* the write. Full list in [oss/cordango/docs/apigenerator-assessment.md](oss/cordango/docs/apigenerator-assessment.md).

**Permissions: two implementations, one contract.** The scaffold has its own resolver. Drift is detected, not prevented — [tests/fixtures/permissions/](oss/cordango/tests/fixtures/permissions/) holds hand-written decisions and *both* suites assert them. Hand-written rather than recorded from your evaluator, because recording makes one side's bugs the definition of correct. Both agree today. I also removed the dangling `Cordango.Authorization` ProjectReference the revert left behind — it was building as a warning nobody reads.

**Three bugs the new tests caught in my own work.** `messages.de.json` and `messages.en.json` were silently compiled into `de/` and `en/` **satellite assemblies** — the SDK reads a dotted segment in a resource name as a culture. Clean build, no warning, and every generated app would have shipped with no German. `Program.cs` registered `AppDbContext` twice, which would have given each request two change trackers. And `PermissionResolver`'s no-roles read-only fallback ran *before* any authentication check — deploying an application whose definition declares no roles would have published every row to anonymous callers.

**Not done, deliberately:** `npm ci && npm run build`. The scaffold's `web/package.json` wants the controls bundle at `file:./vendor/`, and `oss/web-controls/dist` is gitignored — embedding it would break a clean clone rather than fix anything. Vendoring needs a release step and belongs with the Vue emitters at S9.

OSS suite **1,446 green**, including from a copy outside the tree entirely. Platform builds clean; its 561 failures are all `NpgsqlException` — Docker is down, so `docker compose up -d db` when you want the real bar. Web 435 green. All four repos staged.

Next is **S7** — the backend emitters: POCOs, entity configurations, hooks, `AppPermissions`, `CommandService`, and the EF-scaffolded migration with the pinned id.

<script setup>
import { computed, ref } from 'vue'
import { api } from '../api.js'
import { loadRecords } from '../records.js'

const props = defineProps({ field: Object, modelValue: null })
const emit = defineEmits(['update:model-value'])

const value = computed({
  get: () => props.modelValue,
  set: (v) => emit('update:model-value', v),
})

const rules = computed(() => (props.field?.required ? [(v) => !!v || 'Required'] : []))

const inputTypes = {
  date: 'date',
  datetime: 'datetime-local',
  integer: 'number',
  decimal: 'number',
  money: 'number',
  email: 'email',
  url: 'url',
}

const inputType = computed(() => inputTypes[props.field?.type] || 'text')

const suffix = computed(() => {
  if (props.field?.unit) return props.field.unit
  if (props.field?.type === 'money') return props.field.currency || 'EUR'
  return undefined
})

// Reference pickers load their options when the menu first opens, not on mount. A form with six
// references would otherwise fetch six tables before showing the person anything.
const options = ref([])
const loadingOptions = ref(false)

async function loadOptions() {
  if (options.value.length || loadingOptions.value) return
  loadingOptions.value = true
  try {
    const isPerson = props.field.targetApp === 'platform' || props.field.targetEntity === 'person'
    const target = isPerson ? 'directory/person' : props.field.targetEntity
    const page = await loadRecords(target, { take: 200 })
    options.value = (page?.items ?? []).map((r) => ({
      value: r.id,
      title: r.full_name || r.name || r.title || r.description || r.id,
    }))
  } finally {
    loadingOptions.value = false
  }
}

const uploading = ref(false)

async function upload(files) {
  const file = Array.isArray(files) ? files[0] : files
  if (!file) return
  uploading.value = true
  try {
    // The field stores the reference the server hands back, not the file. Content-addressed, so the
    // same document attached twice is stored once.
    const stored = await api.upload(file)
    value.value = stored.reference
  } finally {
    uploading.value = false
  }
}
</script>

<template>
  <v-textarea
    v-if="field.type === 'longtext'"
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
    :rules="rules"
    rows="3"
    auto-grow
  />

  <v-checkbox
    v-else-if="field.type === 'boolean'"
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
  />

  <v-select
    v-else-if="field.type === 'select'"
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
    :rules="rules"
    :items="field.options || []"
    item-title="label"
    item-value="value"
  />

  <v-select
    v-else-if="field.type === 'multiselect'"
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :items="field.options || []"
    item-title="label"
    item-value="value"
    multiple
    chips
  />

  <v-autocomplete
    v-else-if="field.type === 'reference'"
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
    :rules="rules"
    :items="options"
    :loading="loadingOptions"
    @update:menu="loadOptions"
  />

  <v-file-input
    v-else-if="field.type === 'attachment'"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
    :loading="uploading"
    @update:model-value="upload"
  />

  <v-text-field
    v-else
    v-model="value"
    :label="field.label"
    :hint="field.help"
    :rules="rules"
    :type="inputType"
    :suffix="suffix"
  />
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
import { entityOf, createRecord, updateRecord } from '../records.js'
import FieldInput from './FieldInput.vue'

const props = defineProps({ entity: String, record: Object })
const emit = defineEmits(['close', 'saved'])

const open = ref(true)
const busy = ref(false)
const error = ref(null)
const fields = ref({ ...props.record })

const isNew = computed(() => !props.record?.id)
const definition = computed(() => entityOf(props.entity))

// What a person can fill in. System fields are set by the runtime, and fields the definition marks
// hideOnCreate are filled later in the process — putting an approver box on a creation form invites
// somebody to approve their own request.
const shown = computed(() =>
  (definition.value?.fields ?? []).filter(
    (f) => !f.system && !f.readOnly && !(isNew.value && f.hideOnCreate),
  ))

async function save() {
  busy.value = true
  error.value = null
  try {
    const body = {}
    for (const field of shown.value) {
      if (fields.value[field.key] !== undefined) body[field.key] = fields.value[field.key]
    }

    if (isNew.value) await createRecord(props.entity, body)
    else await updateRecord(props.entity, props.record.id, body)

    emit('saved')
  } catch (failure) {
    error.value = failure.message
  } finally {
    busy.value = false
  }
}

function close(value) {
  if (!value) emit('close')
}
</script>

<template>
  <v-dialog v-model="open" max-width="640" @update:model-value="close">
    <v-card>
      <v-card-title>{{ isNew ? 'New ' + (definition?.label || '') : definition?.label }}</v-card-title>
      <v-card-text>
        <FieldInput
          v-for="field in shown"
          :key="field.key"
          :field="field"
          :model-value="fields[field.key]"
          @update:model-value="(v) => (fields[field.key] = v)"
        />
        <v-alert v-if="error" type="error" variant="tonal" class="mt-2">{{ error }}</v-alert>
      </v-card-text>
      <v-card-actions>
        <v-spacer />
        <v-btn variant="text" @click="emit('close')">Cancel</v-btn>
        <v-btn color="primary" :loading="busy" @click="save">Save</v-btn>
      </v-card-actions>
    </v-card>
  </v-dialog>
</template>

s=s.replace('''        Fields = [.. AppModel.Arr(json["fields"]).OfType<JsonObject>().Select(f => new FieldModel(f, Key))];''',
'''        // company_id and app_id never reach the standalone model. The compiler adds them because a
        // platform row has to say which tenant and which application it belongs to; here the answer
        // is the same in every row of every table forever, and a column that always holds one value
        // is a column somebody will eventually filter on and be confused by.
        Fields =
        [
            .. AppModel.Arr(json["fields"]).OfType<JsonObject>()
                .Select(f => new FieldModel(f, Key))
                .Where(f => !FieldModel.DroppedKeys.Contains(f.Key)),
        ];''')
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8',newline='').write(s)

# 2. Descriptor fields get a Descriptor suffix so they never shadow the entity type.
p=r'C:\Work\github\AppBuilder\oss\cordango\src\Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue\Emit\BackendEmitter.cs'

s=s.replace('''            source.Line($"public static readonly RecordDescriptor<{entity.TypeName}> {entity.TypeName} = new(");''',

            // inside the class — nameof(ExpenseClaim.Amount) then resolves against the descriptor
            // rather than the entity, and the error names a property nobody wrote.
            source.Line($"public static readonly RecordDescriptor<{entity.TypeName}> {entity.TypeName}Descriptor = new(");''')
s=s.replace('''            source.Line($"services.AddRecord(AppDescriptors.{entity.TypeName});");''',
            '''            source.Line($"services.AddRecord(AppDescriptors.{entity.TypeName}Descriptor);");''')

1	// Reading and writing records, and turning a stored value into something a person can read.
2	//
3	// Everything the screens need from the server goes through here, so the wire format is decided once.
4	// The shapes it works in — entity keys, field keys, filters — are the App Definition's own, which is
5	// why a screen generated from a definition can be read next to the definition it came from.
6	
7	import { api } from './api.js'
8	import { app } from './app.js'
9	import { session } from './session.js'
10	
11	/** One entity's description, as the definition wrote it. */
12	export const entityOf = (key) => app.entities.find((e) => e.key === key) || null
13	
14	/** One field's description. */
15	export const fieldOf = (entityKey, fieldKey) =>
16	  entityOf(entityKey)?.fields.find((f) => f.key === fieldKey) || null
17	
18	/** One saved view. */
19	export const viewOf = (key) => app.views.find((v) => v.key === key) || null
20	
21	/** The process governing an entity, if one does. */
22	export const processOf = (entityKey) => app.processes.find((p) => p.entity === entityKey) || null
23	
24	/** The commands available on an entity. */
25	export const commandsOf = (entityKey) => app.commands.filter((c) => c.entity === entityKey)
26	
27	/** The field whose value stands for the whole record in a link or a chip. */
28	export function displayOf(entityKey, record) {
29	  if (!record) return ''
30	  const entity = entityOf(entityKey)
31	  const key = entity?.displayField
32	  return String(record?.[key] ?? record?.id ?? '')
33	}
34	
35	/**
36	 * Resolve the placeholders a definition may put in a filter value.
37	 *
38	 * `{{actor.id}}` is the signed-in PERSON, not their login — "expenses I submitted" compares against
39	 * a directory reference, and comparing it against an identity-table key would match nothing, on
40	 * every such view, without any error to notice.
41	 */
42	export function resolveValue(value, context) {
43	  if (typeof value !== 'string') return value
44	
45	  return value
46	    .replace('{{actor.id}}', context?.personId ?? '')
47	    .replace('{{actor.userId}}', context?.userId ?? '')
48	    .replace('{{today}}', new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10))
49	}
50	
51	/**
52	 * Does a block's `visibleWhen` hold right now?
53	 *
54	 * Evaluated in the browser, against the scope the block is in: the record it is bound to, the
55	 * screen's own state, or the person looking at it. That is what lets a section appear only while a
56	 * request is pending, or a day/week toggle swap which grid renders, without a round trip.
57	 *
58	 * A block with no condition is always visible, and a condition naming none of eq/neq/in is too —
59	 * the schema allows it and "shown" is the safer reading of "the author wrote a condition and did not
60	 * say what it tests".
61	 */
62	export function visibleWhen(condition, record, state) {
63	  if (!condition?.value) return true
64	
65	  const resolved = resolveScope(condition.value, record, state)
66	
67	  if ('eq' in condition) return resolved === condition.eq
68	  if ('neq' in condition) return resolved !== condition.neq
69	  if ('in' in condition) return (condition.in || []).includes(resolved)
70	  return true
71	}
72	
73	/** `{{record.status}}`, `{{state.cursor}}`, `{{actor.id}}` — or a literal, unchanged. */
74	function resolveScope(expression, record, state) {
75	  const match = /^\{\{\s*([\w.]+)\s*\}\}$/.exec(expression)
76	  if (!match) return expression
77	
78	  const [scope, ...rest] = match[1].split('.')
79	  const key = rest.join('.')
80	
81	  if (scope === 'record') return record?.[key]
82	  if (scope === 'state') return state?.[key]
83	  if (scope === 'actor') return key === 'id' ? session.personId : session[key]
84	  return undefined
85	}
86	
87	/** Turn a definition filter into the query-string term the API expects. */
88	export const filterTerm = (filter, context) =>
89	  `${filter.field}:${filter.operator}:${resolveValue(filter.value ?? '', context) ?? ''}`
90	
91	/** Turn a definition sort list into the API's `sort` parameter. */
92	export const sortTerm = (sort) =>
93	  (sort || []).map((s) => (s.direction === 'desc' ? `-${s.field}` : s.field)).join(',')
94	
95	/** A page of records for a view. */
96	export async function loadView(view, context, { skip = 0, take = 100, extraFilters = [] } = {}) {
97	  const params = new URLSearchParams()
98	  for (const filter of [...(view.filters || []), ...extraFilters]) {
99	    params.append('filter', filterTerm(filter, context))
100	  }
101	  const sort = sortTerm(view.sort)
102	  if (sort) params.set('sort', sort)
103	  params.set('skip', String(skip))
104	  params.set('take', String(take))
105	
106	  return api.get(`/api/${view.entity}?${params}`)
107	}
108	
109	/** A page of records for an entity, with filters given directly. */
110	export async function loadRecords(entityKey, { filters = [], sort = '', skip = 0, take = 100, context } = {}) {
111	  const params = new URLSearchParams()
112	  for (const filter of filters) params.append('filter', filterTerm(filter, context))
113	  if (sort) params.set('sort', sort)
114	  params.set('skip', String(skip))
115	  params.set('take', String(take))
116	  return api.get(`/api/${entityKey}?${params}`)
117	}
118	
119	export const loadRecord = (entityKey, id) => api.get(`/api/${entityKey}/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`)
120	export const createRecord = (entityKey, body) => api.post(`/api/${entityKey}`, body)
121	export const updateRecord = (entityKey, id, body) => api.patch(`/api/${entityKey}/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, body)
122	export const deleteRecord = (entityKey, id) => api.delete(`/api/${entityKey}/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`)
123	
124	/** Run a command against one record. */
125	export const runCommand = (entityKey, id, command, input) =>
126	  api.post(`/api/${entityKey}/${encodeURIComponent(id)}/commands/${command}`, input ?? {})
127	
128	/**
129	 * An aggregate over an entity — what a stat and a chart both need.
130	 *
131	 * Computed on the server, because a figure over a hundred thousand rows must not require the

134	export async function loadAggregate(source, context) {

# {{AppName}} � one image serving the API and the single-page app from the same origin.
#
# Same origin is a decision, not an accident. It is what lets the session live in a cookie with no
# CORS configuration to get wrong, and what lets the antiforgery token be read by this application's
# own script and by nothing else. Splitting the two across origins is possible and costs you both.

# ---- the front end -------------------------------------------------------------------------
FROM node:22-alpine AS web
WORKDIR /src/web

# Dependencies first, so that editing a component does not re-run the install.
#
# `npm ci` when there is a lock file, because it installs exactly what the lock file says and fails
# if the two have drifted � which is what you want from a build you expect to reproduce. A freshly
# generated application has no lock file yet: a lock file records a resolution against the registry,
# and the generator does not go to the network. Run `npm install` once in web/ and commit the result,
# and every build after that is the reproducible one.
COPY web/package.json web/package-lock.json* ./
RUN if [ -f package-lock.json ]; then npm ci; else npm install; fi

COPY web/ ./
RUN npm run build

# ---- the back end --------------------------------------------------------------------------
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS api
WORKDIR /src

COPY api/*.csproj ./api/
RUN dotnet restore ./api

COPY api/ ./api/
COPY --from=web /src/api/wwwroot ./api/wwwroot
RUN dotnet publish ./api -c Release -o /app --no-restore

# ---- what actually ships -------------------------------------------------------------------
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0
WORKDIR /app

# Not root. A web process has no business being able to write to its own binaries, and the one
# directory it does need to write to is named below.
RUN useradd --uid 5678 --create-home app \
    && mkdir -p /appdata/media \
    && chown -R app /appdata
USER app

COPY --from=api /app .

ENV ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS=8080 \
    Storage__Path=/appdata/media
EXPOSE 8080

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s \
    CMD wget --spider -q http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "{{AppNamespace}}.Api.dll"]

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue'
import { useRouter } from 'vue-router'
import { api } from '../api.js'

const router = useRouter()
const items = ref([])
const unread = ref(0)
const open = ref(false)

async function load() {
  try {
    const page = await api.get('/api/notifications')
    items.value = page?.items ?? []
    unread.value = page?.unread ?? 0
  } catch {
    // Not signed in, or the server is unreachable. A bell that throws would take the whole shell
    // down with it, and the one thing it is not is important enough for that.
  }
}

async function openItem(item) {
  open.value = false
  if (!item.read_at) {
    await api.post(`/api/notifications/${item.id}/read`).catch(() => {})
    unread.value = Math.max(0, unread.value - 1)
    item.read_at = new Date().toISOString()
  }
  if (item.link) router.push(item.link)
}

async function readAll() {
  await api.post('/api/notifications/read-all').catch(() => {})
  await load()
}

// Polled rather than pushed. A websocket would be better and is a dependency and a deployment
// concern; a minute is soon enough for "your expense was approved" and costs one small query.
let timer = null
onMounted(() => {
  load()
  timer = setInterval(load, 60_000)
})
onUnmounted(() => clearInterval(timer))
</script>

<template>
  <v-menu v-model="open" :close-on-content-click="false" location="bottom end">
    <template #activator="{ props }">
      <v-btn icon v-bind="props" @click="load">
        <v-badge :model-value="unread > 0" :content="unread" color="error">
          <v-icon icon="mdi-bell-outline" />
        </v-badge>
      </v-btn>
    </template>

    <v-card min-width="360" max-width="440">
      <v-card-title class="d-flex align-center text-subtitle-1">
        Notifications
        <v-spacer />
        <v-btn v-if="unread > 0" size="x-small" variant="text" @click="readAll">Mark all read</v-btn>
      </v-card-title>

      <v-list v-if="items.length" density="compact" max-height="400" class="overflow-y-auto">
        <v-list-item
          v-for="item in items"
          :key="item.id"
          :active="!item.read_at"
          @click="openItem(item)"
        >
          <v-list-item-title>{{ item.title }}</v-list-item-title>
          <v-list-item-subtitle>{{ item.message }}</v-list-item-subtitle>
        </v-list-item>
      </v-list>

      <v-card-text v-else class="text-medium-emphasis">Nothing yet.</v-card-text>
    </v-card>
  </v-menu>
</template>

attachment.snippet:
1	# {{AppName}}
2	
3	Generated by [Cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango) from an App Definition, and yours from
4	here on.
5	
6	This is an ordinary ASP.NET Core + EF Core + PostgreSQL application with a Vue 3 and Vuetify front
7	end. Nothing in it calls home, nothing requires the tool that produced it, and every file is one you
8	can read, change and deploy anywhere .NET runs.
9	{{PartialBuildSection}}
10	## Running it
11	
12	```
13	cp .env.example .env      # set DB_PASSWORD, ADMIN_EMAIL, ADMIN_PASSWORD
14	docker compose up --build
15	```
16	
17	Then open <http://localhost:8080> and sign in as the administrator you named in `.env`.
18	
19	`ADMIN_EMAIL` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` are read once, on the first start with an empty database, to
20	create the first account. There is no default password: an application that shipped with one would
21	ship compromised.
22	
23	## Running it without Docker
24	
25	```
26	# database
27	docker compose up -d db
28	
29	# back end
30	cd api && dotnet run
31	
32	# front end, in another terminal
33	cd web && npm install && npm run dev
34	```
35	
36	`npm run dev` proxies `/api` to the back end so the two behave as one origin, which is how they are
37	served in production.
38	
39	## How it is laid out
40	
41	```
42	api/                  the ASP.NET Core application
43	  Program.cs          startup: database, identity, the runtime, the pipeline
44	  AppSetup.cs         every entity, hook and permission, registered — generated
45	  Data/               the DbContext and one configuration per entity — generated
46	  Entities/           one plain class per entity — generated
47	  Controllers/        one per entity — generated
48	  Migrations/         EF migrations. Ordinary ones: read them, edit them, review them
49	  Identity/           sign-in, accounts, the first administrator
50	  Cordango/           the Cordango runtime, as source (Apache-2.0)
51	  Resources/          messages.en.json, messages.de.json
52	web/                  the Vue application
53	  src/app.js          your definition, as the screens read it — generated
54	  src/pages/          one component per screen and per record — generated
55	  src/blocks/         the building blocks those pages are made of
56	Dockerfile            one image, API and front end on one origin
57	docker-compose.yml    the application and a pinned Postgres
58	cordango.build.json   what produced this, and every file it wrote
59	```
60	
61	## Regenerating
62	
63	Running the generator again over the same output directory replaces the files it wrote last time and
64	leaves everything else alone. `cordango.build.json` lists exactly which files those are, so there is
65	never a guess about what is safe to edit.
66	
67	Files marked *generated* above will be overwritten. To change what they contain, change the App
68	Definition. To add behaviour, add files of your own beside them — a hook registered in its own file,
69	a controller with its own route, a page the router picks up. That is the intended way to extend a
70	generated application, and it survives every rebuild.
71	
72	## Changing the schema
73	
74	After generation this is a normal EF Core project:
75	
76	```
77	cd api
78	dotnet ef migrations add WhateverYouChanged
79	```
80	
81	The application applies pending migrations at startup.
82	
83	## Who may do what
84	
85	Permissions come from the definition's roles and are compiled into `AppPermissions.cs`: which
86	entities a role may read, create, change and delete, which fields it may see or set, and which
87	commands it may run. The rules are enforced on every route, and a field a role cannot read never
88	appears in a response — not in the record, and not in a message rendered from it.
89	
90	Two things are decided outside the definition, because the definition has nothing to say about them:
91	
92	- **Signing in** is stock ASP.NET Core Identity with a cookie. Swap it for single sign-on by
93	  changing `api/Identity/AppIdentity.cs`.
94	- **The `Administrator` role** bypasses definition roles entirely. It is an ASP.NET role rather than
95	  a definition role, so reading the definition never turns up a role that grants more than it says.
96	
97	## What is not generated yet
98	
99	`cordango.build.json` lists it exactly, under `unsupportedCapabilities`, and the section above
100	appears in this README when there is anything to report. As of this build the generator does not yet
101	emit **workflows**, **computed fields and rollups**, **command guards**, or the **email and webhook**
102	effects. In-app **notifications** are generated and do work.
103	
104	A build that needs any of those refuses unless you pass `--allow-incomplete`, so an application that
105	was built completely is one you can trust to be complete.
106	
107	## Security worth knowing about
108	
109	- Every state-changing request requires an antiforgery token, enforced globally rather than per
110	  controller — including on a controller you add later without reading this.
111	- The front-end client in `web/src/api.js` attaches the token automatically. Anything that talks to
112	  the API should go through it.
113	- Uploaded files are addressed by the hash of their contents, so a reference cannot be guessed or
114	  enumerated. Any signed-in caller who *has* a reference can fetch the file behind it, including one
115	  attached to a record their role cannot read.

and a deterministic demo dataset.

**Pages are EXPANDED, not interpreted.** A block tree could go to a runtime renderer and that would
be less code; it would also mean somebody who wants to change a screen has nothing to edit. So the
tree becomes a real Vue file — `<BlockRow><StatCard …/><StatCard …/></BlockRow>` — over block
components that ship in the scaffold. Readable, diffable, and yours the moment you stop
regenerating.

**The migration is verified by EF itself.** The plan wanted `MigrationsScaffolder` in-process, which
needs the compiled entity classes the generator is still deciding on. Instead the schema is derived
once and both the migration and the model snapshot are written from it — and a test then generates
an application, builds it, runs `dotnet ef migrations add` and **asserts the resulting migration is
EMPTY**. An empty diff is EF saying our snapshot describes its model exactly, which is the only
thing that matters: a snapshot that is nearly right makes the user's first real migration full of
`AlterColumn` calls that change nothing. It caught two while being written — nullable value types
spelled without the `?`, and the directory tables having drifted from what the runtime configures.
The Identity migration does not vary per app, so it was scaffolded once by `dotnet ef` and lifted
into the scaffold as template data, id pinned.

and webhook effects yet. Those would be INVISIBLE in a running application — an approval that
silently sends no notification looks fine — so the build now refuses unless you pass
`--allow-incomplete`, and a permitted build carries the list in `cordango.build.json` and in a
**Partial build** section at the top of the generated README. The flag was `--allow-partial-ui`; that
name assumed the only gap would be a screen nobody could draw, and behaviour can be missing too. Old
spelling still works.

server: an in-app notification table, a bell in the shell, templates rendered from the record after
the command wrote to it. So expenses builds with no warnings at all; time-off reports one timeline
block and is otherwise complete.

ten operators of near-identical generated code, in every application, all needing regeneration to fix
one bug — versus one expression builder driven by the property name the descriptor already carries.

field key that is not in the descriptor is refused by name rather than interpolated anywhere.

# Copy to .env and fill in. .env is gitignored; keep it that way.

# The database password. No default, on purpose.
DB_PASSWORD=

# Read once, on the first start with an empty database, to create the first account.
# After an administrator exists these are ignored.
ADMIN_EMAIL=
ADMIN_PASSWORD=

# The port the application is published on.
PORT=8080

# Load the generated demo dataset on a fresh database. Set to false for a real deployment.
SEED=true

# Set to "today" to re-anchor the demo dates on the day it loads. The dataset is otherwise
# reproducible: the same build always produces the same rows on the same dates.
SEED_DATE=
=== compose ===
# Everything Expenses needs to run, on one machine.
#
# Two services and one volume. The database version is pinned rather than floating on `latest`,
# because a Postgres major upgrade is a decision to make deliberately on a Tuesday morning and not
# one to discover after a `docker compose pull`.

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.5-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: expenses
      POSTGRES_USER: expenses
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - db:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U expenses"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  app:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      # The application migrates its own schema at startup, so it needs a database that is ready to
      # answer rather than merely a container that has been created.
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      ConnectionStrings__Database: "Host=db;Port=5432;Database=expenses;Username=expenses;Password=${DB_PASSWORD}"
      # Read once, on the first start, to create the first administrator. After that it is ignored.
      # Load the generated demo dataset on a fresh database. Once the tables have rows this does
      # nothing, so it is safe to leave on — set SEED=false to skip it entirely.
      Seed__Enabled: ${SEED:-true}
      Seed__Date: ${SEED_DATE:-}
      Admin__Email: ${ADMIN_EMAIL:-}
      Admin__Password: ${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}
    ports:
      - "${PORT:-8080}:8080"
    volumes:
      - media:/appdata/media

volumes:
  db:
  media:

The generator now emits a whole application, and it builds.

```
cd oss/examples/expenses
dotnet run --project ../../cordango/src/Cordango.Cli -- \
    build --app expenses --target standalone --out C:/tmp/expenses-app

cd C:/tmp/expenses-app
cp .env.example .env        # DB_PASSWORD, ADMIN_EMAIL, ADMIN_PASSWORD
docker compose up --build   # then http://localhost:8080
```

102 files. `dotnet build api` and `npm run build` are both green — asserted by tests that run the real SDK over the real output, not by inspecting strings. **It has been built, not run** — Docker is down here, so the live pass is yours. It comes seeded with 24 expense claims across all four states and twelve people, so the screens have something on them.

**Pages are expanded into real Vue, not handed to a runtime renderer.** A renderer would have been less code and would have left you nothing to edit; `OverviewPage.vue` is `<BlockRow><StatCard …/></BlockRow>` over components that ship in the scaffold, and it's yours the moment you stop regenerating.

**The migration is certified by EF rather than by care.** In-process `MigrationsScaffolder` needs the compiled entity classes, which don't exist while the generator is deciding what they'll say — so the schema is derived once, both the migration and the snapshot are written from it, and then a test generates an app, builds it, runs `dotnet ef migrations add` and **asserts the result is empty**. An empty diff is EF saying our snapshot describes its model exactly, which is what keeps your first real migration from being full of `AlterColumn` calls that change nothing. It caught two while being written. The Identity schema doesn't vary per app, so I scaffolded it once with `dotnet ef` and lifted it in as template data.

**What's missing is loud, and that's the part I'd want you to check.** Workflows, computed fields, command guards and email/webhook effects aren't emitted — and those are invisible in a running application, so a build needing any of them now **refuses** unless you pass `--allow-incomplete`, which scars `cordango.build.json` and puts a *Partial build* section at the top of the README. `notify` I implemented rather than warned about (in-app notification table, bell in the shell), because it needed no mail server and it's what makes expenses build clean. `time-off` reports one timeline block and is otherwise complete.

I renamed `--allow-partial-ui` to `--allow-incomplete` — the old name assumed the only possible gap was a screen nobody could draw. Old spelling still works.

**`@cordango/web-controls` isn't used by generated apps.** The blocks are Vuetify directly, which means the vendoring blocker I flagged last time — `dist` is gitignored, nothing to vendor without a release step — simply went away. Moving generated apps onto the package is a later refinement and takes that question with it.

Four defects found by building the output rather than trusting it: `appsettings.json` shipped `""` so `??` never fired and a missing connection string became an Npgsql parse error twenty frames deeper; a generated descriptor field named after its own entity type **shadowed** it, so `nameof(ExpenseClaim.Amount)` resolved against the descriptor; the Dockerfile created an `app` user the aspnet image already has and health-checked with `wget`, which that image doesn't ship; and `company_id`/`app_id` were still reaching the standalone model.

OSS suite **1,476 green**, including from a clone with no platform above it. Platform green except the 561 database-backed tests — all `NpgsqlException`, Docker is down. Web 435 green. All staged.

# Cordango examples

Four complete Cordango applications, as source you can clone, read, change and build.

> Status: pre-alpha. These track the App Definition schema in
> [cordango/cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango) and will move while it settles.

Each directory is a real workspace, not a snippet. What you see is what an author writes: one file
per aggregate, an entity here, a lifecycle there, a role, a screen. No compiled App Definition is
checked in, because that is the output of the toolchain rather than the thing a person edits.

```
cd expenses
cordango check                        # parse, lower and validate. No model, no database.
cordango inspect                      # what is in here
cordango check --target standalone    # can this be generated as an application you own?
```

## The examples

| Example | Entities | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`expenses/`](expenses) | 1 | The smallest complete application, and the one to read first. An approval lifecycle, and three roles that see genuinely different things. |
| [`time-off/`](time-off) | 1 | Absence requests with a manager approval step, a team schedule, and a duration the application works out for itself. |
| [`task-manager/`](task-manager) | 5 | Projects, tasks, subtasks and milestones, with rollups that let a parent count its children. Read this one for computed fields. |
| [`room-booking/`](room-booking) | 4 | Rooms, bookings, attendees, and a policy entity that holds the rules instead of hard-coding them. |

## Reading one

Start with `apps/<name>/app.cordango.yaml`, which names the application and fixes the order things
