content.text:
The app is at [oss/examples/expenses/generated/](oss/examples/expenses/generated/). Start with [ExpenseClaim.cs](oss/examples/expenses/generated/api/Entities/ExpenseClaim.cs), [AppRoles.cs](oss/examples/expenses/generated/api/Security/AppRoles.cs), [AppCommands.cs](oss/examples/expenses/generated/api/Commands/AppCommands.cs) and [OverviewPage.vue](oss/examples/expenses/generated/web/src/pages/OverviewPage.vue) — those four are the whole idea. Note it's gitignored: the examples repo already has `/*/generated/` excluded, from the earlier decision that compiled output isn't checked in. Say the word if you'd rather it were committed as a showcase.

**On migrations — you're right that it would cover it, and that's the honest starting point.** `UseAutomaticApiMigrations` diffs the model against the live database at every startup and issues the DDL. Zero migration emitter, zero snapshot, zero fidelity test. I'd have saved about 400 lines. Four things stopped me:

**There's no artifact to review.** The DDL is computed at startup against whatever the production database happens to look like. You cannot see, before deploying, what it's about to do.

**Data loss is the default in that wrapper.** `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` takes an `AutomaticMigrationDataLossAllowed` flag, and `ServiceExtension.UseAutomaticApiMigrations` hard-codes it `true` on the first call *regardless of the `allowDataLoss` argument the caller passed* — then swallows `MigrateDatabaseException` to `Console.WriteLine` and continues with a wrong schema. Renaming a field in a definition is a drop-and-add. That's someone's expense history gone on a deploy nobody reviewed.

**It's a one-way door for the person who owns the app.** No `__EFMigrationsHistory`, no baseline. The day they need a real migration — backfill before a NOT NULL, rename by copy, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` — they can't, and there's no path back to being able to. EF's own `EnsureCreated()` has exactly the same problem, and its docs say so.

**And it puts a third-party package on the critical path of an app they own forever.** `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` has to track every EF major for as long as the app lives.

So the trade I took: ~400 lines of emitter, and in exchange `docker compose up --build` works on a fresh clone *and* `dotnet ef migrations add` works correctly from day one. The fidelity test is what makes the second half true rather than hopeful — [00000000000001_InitialCreate.cs](oss/examples/expenses/generated/api/Migrations/00000000000001_InitialCreate.cs) is a file you can read, and EF itself certifies the snapshot beside it by producing an empty diff.

One alternative I should name because it's genuinely cleaner than what I built: **emit no migration at all and have the README say "run `dotnet ef migrations add Initial` once"**. Fully EF-native, no emitter, no snapshot, no test. The only thing it costs is that the first run needs an SDK command before `docker compose up` works — which is precisely the thing you asked me to make work. If you'd rather have the simpler generator and accept that one manual step, it's a small change and I'd do it.

# Cordango.Standalone

The runtime a [Cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango)-generated standalone application runs
on.

You do not usually install this yourself. `cordango build --target standalone` generates an
application that references it, and everything in it exists to serve code the generator emits
alongside: typed record entities, an `IEntityTypeConfiguration` per entity, one controller per
entity, and the definition's roles as compiled rules.

## What is in it

- **Records.** `IRecord`, `IHasTrackingFields`, and a generic store that runs lifecycle hooks and
  stamps who wrote a row and when — in one place, where the type system checks it.
- **Hooks.** Six interfaces resolved from the service container rather than implemented on the
  entity, because in a generated application the entity file is the one the generator overwrites.
- **Permissions.** An App Definition's `roles` resolved to an effective answer: union across roles,
  a specific grant beating the wildcard, field rules resolved per role before unioning, and commands
  denied unless granted.
- **Queries.** Filtering, sorting and aggregates built once from the field keys a descriptor carries,
  so an application does not carry sixteen field types times ten operators of generated comparisons.
- **A directory.** People, departments, groups, organizations and contacts — what a reference to a
  person points at when there is no platform to point at.
- **The wire.** `{code, error}` responses, global antiforgery, content-addressed file storage.

## Licence

Apache-2.0. The application generated around it is yours, unencumbered.

content.text:
Both done.

**`Cordango.Standalone` is a real NuGet package now** — id, version, licence expression, repo URL, README, symbols. `dotnet pack` produces `Cordango.Standalone.0.1.0-alpha.nupkg` and its `.snupkg` today. It can't be *restored* until it's published, so the generated app gets the same source as a **sibling project** instead of a directory inside itself:

```
api/        your application — 24 files, all yours
runtime/    the Cordango runtime, own csproj, own version
```

[`api/Expenses.Api.csproj`](oss/examples/expenses/generated/api/Expenses.Api.csproj) has one `ProjectReference` and, above it, the exact line to replace it with. `--runtime package` emits that shape today for anyone whose feed already has it, and there's a test on both shapes so the option can't quietly rot while nobody can exercise it.

**Migrations: no manual step, and that was already true.** `docker compose up --build`, or `docker compose up -d db && dotnet run` — the app migrates itself on the way up. I also made the failure mode readable: Npgsql's own message names a socket and reads like a bug in your application, so startup now catches it and says *"start it with `docker compose up -d db`"*.

Since you asked specifically, the four reasons I didn't take `UseAutomaticApiMigrations` — it *would* have got you here with ~400 fewer lines:

- **Nothing to review.** The DDL is computed at startup against production. You can't see what it's about to do.
- **The wrapper hard-codes `AutomaticMigrationDataLossAllowed = true`** regardless of the argument passed, then swallows the failure to `Console.WriteLine`. A renamed field is a drop-and-add on a deploy nobody read.
- **One-way door.** No `__EFMigrationsHistory`, so the day the owner needs a real migration — backfill before a NOT NULL, rename by copy, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` — there's no path to one. EF's own `EnsureCreated()` has exactly the same problem and its docs say so.
- It puts a third-party package on the critical path of an app someone owns for years.

The generated app is at [oss/examples/expenses/generated/](oss/examples/expenses/generated/) — **note it's gitignored**, from the earlier decision that compiled output doesn't get committed to the examples repo. Say the word if you'd rather it were committed as a showcase.

OSS suite **1,478 green**, including from a clone with no platform above it. Everything staged.

content.text:
`docker compose up --build` now works with nothing configured. Pull the latest generated app (I refreshed [oss/examples/expenses/generated/](oss/examples/expenses/generated/)) and try again.

**`DB_PASSWORD` gets a default**, and that's safe specifically here: the `db` service publishes no port, so the only thing that can reach Postgres is the app container on the compose network. The comment says exactly that, and says to set a real one before it leaves your machine — particularly before anyone adds a `ports:` mapping for debugging.

**The admin password I did not default**, because a constant would mean every application this toolchain ever produces ships with the same one. Instead it's **generated on first start and printed once**:

```
docker compose logs app | grep -A4 "FIRST ADMINISTRATOR"
```

```
==================== FIRST ADMINISTRATOR ====================
  email:    admin@localhost
  password: 7xQm-vK3nRt2wY9pAeZf
  Generated because Admin__Password was not set. It is not stored anywhere
  in readable form and will not be shown again. Change it after signing in.
============================================================
```

Twenty characters from `RandomNumberGenerator` — not `Random`, which is seeded from the clock and would have two containers starting in the same second agree on the answer. Built to satisfy the password policy by construction rather than generated-and-retried, and with `I`/`l`/`1`/`O`/`0` left out because someone is going to read it out of a terminal and type it into a browser. Set `ADMIN_EMAIL`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD` in `.env` to choose them yourself; both are still read only once, on a fresh database, and never reset an existing password.

The README's opening is now just the one command, and it says where to find the credentials.
